en: The Mahāvaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: Lamentation. Chapter One: Lamentation. First.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying between the twin śāla trees in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, at the place where the Mallas were born.
At that time, as the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the venerable Ānanda, saying:
"When the Tathāgata appeared in the world and entered parinirvāṇa, what were the original auspicious omens?
Is it not as if we can now see and hear those responses and manifestations among the grove of trees?"
"Please answer my question.
At that time, Ānanda replied to the Buddha in verse:
"I pray you, listen to my dream; its colors were nearly strange to behold."
Recalling what I saw in the night, my heart was secretly filled with perilous fear.
In this Jambudvīpa, I dreamed of a tree of most marvelous growth, fashioned from an interlacing of the seven treasures;
its flowers and fruits were always abundant and flourishing.
It covers the Buddha-worlds, its shade pure and cool;
it awakens and inspires leaping joy, extinguishing all sorrows and ailments.
Its upward movement is infinitely high, and its sublime features are likewise beyond counting.
Those who see him have their eyes purified; those who hear him have their ears attuned to all sounds.
From the tree issue immeasurable tones—the pure sound of the Dharma—which, being fully endowed with emptiness, quiescence, and cessation, bring peace to all beings.
That tree emits a great radiance, Shining everywhere throughout the lands of the East,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; It likewise illumines the ten directions,
Providing protection and rescue for all wriggling creatures.
All who are touched by this light attain inconceivable peace and security.
From the trees emerge various sublime fragrances, and the vessels contain a hundred different varieties;
those who smell these fragrances shall never again fall into the evil realms.
Those in the hells, among the animals, And those upon the path of hungry ghosts— Upon smelling this fragrance, they quickly attain rebirth in a favorable realm.
Such is the virtue of the Great Tree: It enwraps and nourishes all classes of sentient beings.
Suddenly, amidst the trees, he vanished into the earth before the Mallas.
At that time, countless thousands of beings, beyond measure,
wept with profound grief and longing, like the blind who have lost their sight.
No longer hearing their sounds, nor seeing the forms of the trees, and likewise not smelling their fragrance, one is as empty and debilitated as a starving man.
One’s hair stands on end with terror; such dread is brought about by the state of one's mind.
“In a dream last night, such as this occurred; we pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for us.

At that time, the deva of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Guide, the Son of Māra, each accompanied by a multitude of eighty nayutas, arrived together at the grove where the Malla clan was born. They approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated themselves in homage, and withdrew to stand to one side. Simultaneously raising their voices, they addressed the Venerable Ānanda in verse:
“The Honored Deva has now entered parinirvāṇa; does Ānanda not know this?”
Alas! How poignant is this grief; the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa.
The Great Armor obscures ignorance; the Buddha now desires to pass into extinction.
When the World-Honored One enters parinirvāṇa, we shall be far removed from his protection.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses for the sake of the sons of the gods, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, the son of Māra, and the guides:
"Do not grieve or be distressed; The dream you saw is nothing other than this:
Between the twin trees, I shall now enter parinirvāṇa."
The most excellent among trees, wondrous beyond measure,
with light and fragrance most abundant, has vanished beneath the thickets.
The World-Honored One is like a great tree, yet he now dwells amidst the thickets.
In sleep and rest there is no consciousness, like fire extinguished by water.
All things are impermanent; when dharmas arise, they must perish.
This is what the Hero of the World has realized, and for this reason he speaks it for the sake of humanity.
Ānanda, do you know? The World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa; he has sent for the bhikṣu Cālikā, whose wisdom penetrates to the further shore.
Ānanda, go now and deliver this command to Śuddhodana:
The Venerable Aniruddha, whose far-reaching vision is the perfection of transcendent insight;
Ānanda, who proclaims the teachings; Kauṣṭhila, Kātyāyana, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, and Upāli.
Subhūti, Mukharāja, Svāgata, Buddha, Bakula, Nanda, and Megha; Pūrṇa, Māṭhara, Aśvajit,
and all the bhikṣus— Come to deliver those who are terrified.
"Go quickly and inform everyone, so that they may know of my parinirvāṇa.
At that time, Ānanda replied to the World-Honored One in verse:
"My body is utterly exhausted, like a person who is hungry and emaciated."
Hearing that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, I am so overcome with grief that I cannot endure it;
my body is devoid of strength, and my mouth can utter no word;
my mind is further emboldened by cowardice— how shall the Eye of the World proceed?
I cannot bear to inform the Venerable One; this world is not to be thought upon.
As soon as it is seen, it vanishes; we have forever lost his protection.
Without protection, there is extreme suffering—how can I bear to go and inform him?
Hearing this question, how could the Venerable One endure such terror?
The great light of the world has been extinguished so swiftly;
the passing from the world was so sudden that the world has fallen into the blindness of calamity.
"I cannot bear to go before the Elder to report these bitter and poisonous matters.
I pray that the Perfectly Awakened One will send someone else instead, so that there shall be no one left in sorrow.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke this verse for Ānanda:
“Ānanda, weeping with immense sorrow, The palace and its halls are now empty, void of gods and men;
He proclaims to the bhikṣus: ‘It is the constant duty of an attendant.’”
Niti said: "Those who come later shall receive no benefit, only bitter grief.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha was on the summit of Mount Sumeru, extensively expounding the Dharma for the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Seeing the various great and venerable sons of gods, each departing from their palaces in a state of restless unease, Aniruddha thought to himself:

"For what reason have these sons of gods abandoned the pleasures of celestial maidens? Why are they hurrying up and down, some flying and others running, with their retinues scattered and their dwellings empty and suddenly no longer visible?"
At that time, Aniruddha saw from the summit of Mount Sumeru the ground below Mount Ratnākara. Thereupon, standing upon the peak of Sumeru, he raised his voice and praised the Buddha in verse, saying:
“Guiding and benefiting the masses, Bestowing peace and security upon the world, The Perfectly Awakened One is the protector of all beings— How can you pass into *nirvāṇa* so soon?”

Alas! The World-Honored One is like parents; he is the eye of the world that dispels all darkness, and the skilled physician of the world who heals all ailments. Now the Hero of the World has entered parinirvāṇa.
Seeing those who harbor lust and anger as if they were heedless, awakening the ignorant to sever birth and death;
honoring the Dharma above all to bring grief to stinginess and greed, causing them to leave behind hatred and strife and establish themselves in the Great Way.
The Honored One among Gods of Gods, with his golden right arm, Wipes away all [defilements] and bestows the true precepts;
The Buddha causes this land to quake in six ways, And a great sound is heard throughout the entire world.
Just as when a great mountain of rock suddenly collapses, its roar spreads far and wide so that those who hear it tremble;
so now the Hero of the World enters *nirvāṇa*, and his voice resounds through distant lands, causing them to wither with grief.
The demonic armies raise various evil transformations, with vajra weapons beyond counting.
Some wear great mountains or carry fire, yet the World Hero’s majestic radiance does not cause his hair to stir;
he has subdued the hosts of wrathful and harmful Mara-demons, attained the trace of the nectar of immortality, and is free from sorrow or fear.
Having turned the Wheel of Dharma to explain the Four Truths, today the Honored Hero enters Parinirvana.
The World-Honored One manifests countless transformations, making the three thousandfold world-system as a single hair;
he is able to ensure that sentient beings suffer no harm, yet today the Honored Hero enters parinirvāṇa.
Today, Zhongtian came to enter, arriving at the birthplace of the Mallas;
surrounded by a retinue of five hundred, he entered nirvana between the twin trees.
The Buddha, the God among Gods, for a hundred lifetimes past, Has practiced the four dhyānas to deliver and transform sentient beings;
Through the path he has cultivated, he has spread the nectar of immortality, And I am now the last to witness the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
In his comings and goings, he was free from birth and death; in his wise giving, he felt no regret;
in his observance of the true precepts, he was without flattery or deceit; I saw the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa for the last time.
Throughout hundreds of millions of kalpas, no one has ever surpassed him in the vigor of his practice;
his patience is immeasurable, like the earth. I shall now behold the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha, the most honored among gods, in whatever place he is born, Makes offerings to billions of awakened ones;
having attained the track of ambrosia with a mind fixed in unity, I shall now behold the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha, the most honored among devas, in whatever place he is born, possesses supreme wisdom and has realized the three types of supernormal knowledge;
as a Hero of the World throughout the ten directions, he is free from all hindrance—now I shall witness the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Possessing great power equal to all ten [directions], peerless in supernormal powers, he stands as a Vajra;
though one seeks a peer, none can be found—none who are his equal. I shall now behold the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The World Hero, adorned with the body of the ten powers, Wheresoever he turns, his radiance is majestic;
In his every movement and step, he is like a golden mold— I shall now behold the Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa.
Transforming billions of nayutas, establishing them on the path to realization; extinguishing all desires until no dust or defilement remains;
delivering beings from birth and death and burning away their diligent suffering—I shall now behold the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Billions of devas stand in the void, raining down *kubjaka* flowers of various colors;
they rain down diverse, famous incenses, their celestial fragrance wafting abroad. Thus, I shall now behold the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

The Buddha, the Honored One among men, whether walking, standing, or entering a city and treading upon its threshold, grants eyes to the blind so they may behold all forms; I shall now see the Buddha enter into parinirvāṇa.
When the Buddha, the Honored One among Men, stepped through the gate, the sick were healed and filled with joyful exultation;
all attained peace and security, liberated from toil and suffering, as they beheld the Buddha entering nirvana.
When the Buddha entered the city, those in confinement were released; they attained long-lasting peace and joy.
Grief and suffering were extinguished as his supreme wisdom shone forth; I shall henceforth behold the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
His body knows no aging and has no fear of death; having been liberated from all obstructions, his wisdom is peerless.
Among men, there is none superior to the Buddha, the Great Ancestor; I shall now witness the Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa.
The World-Honored One of Ten Powers ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
He delivered his mother, Māyā, establishing her in the wondrous Path, And transformed incalculable hundreds of millions of devas; I shall henceforth behold the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The seventh Brahmā dwells amidst the doubts of the multitude; the Buddha’s realm is vast, yet he bestows the truth of the Way.
That king threw himself down to prostrate in homage, saying: "From this day forth, I shall witness the Buddha's entry into parinirvāṇa."
There were fierce bandits whose power of transgression was strong; you brought down those who would harm others onto the path of ambrosia.
You received into the fold countless people of heterodox arts; I have now seen the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa.
Devadatta harbored poison and his fierce rage was intense; he drove forth a rutting elephant whose strength was difficult to withstand.
The Buddha subdued it within the great city; I shall now witness the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha, guiding people through the Dharma amidst the great assembly, can move heaven and earth and shake the mountains and hills;
the great ocean surges and the aquatic creatures are agitated—now I shall see the Buddha enter Nirvana.

When Aniruddha had spoken this verse, the Buddha immediately manifested his majestic spiritual power, causing all the bhikṣus throughout Jambudvīpa—except for those in the retinue of Mahākāśyapa—to come and assemble at that very moment.

The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and other multitudes throughout the trichiliocosm all went together to the birthplace of the Malla and approached the Buddha’s dwelling to prostrate themselves. They all wept bitterly, raising their voices to call out for the Buddha; their longing was so overwhelming that they felt as if they had lost their own parents. Some drew one another close and wailed together; others looked back at each other and shed tears. Some beat their hands against their thighs or struck their heads; some opened and closed their eyes, their faculties undergoing transformation, their faces and cheeks becoming haggard, their healthy complexion fading into emaciated wrinkles. Some walked backward, placing their right knees on the ground, sighing and wiping away their tears as their lamentations flowed crosswise. In their sorrowful praise of the Buddha, they all cried out in bitter pain: "Alas, Hero of the World!"
Alas, Great Physician! Alas, Lion! Alas, Dharma King!
Alas, King of the Sun and Moon!
Alas, Awakened One, Perfectly Enlightened One!
Alas, Great Radiance, Bestower of Ambrosia!
Thus did the one named Immeasurable Trace wail; some threw themselves down and beat their breasts against the ground, while others covered their faces and struck the earth with their palms.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, knelt with his knees pressed together and his hands resting on the ground, and looking up toward the Buddha, spoke this verse:
"Beholding the multitude wailing and longing [for you], All are possessed by the poison of sorrow."
Each one wails and weeps in sorrow, which only increases my bitter anguish.
It is like a merchant traveling on a journey who encounters fierce bandits midway,
or sees the glare of a great fire, fearing his straw will be scorched to ashes.
Because of seeing the blazing fire, his heart was filled with terror;
his mind harbored trembling dread, and he prostrated before Heaven seeking its compassion.
My own feelings of diligence are boundless, and how can I bear this heavy, stifling sorrow?
Furthermore, I see the common people, wailing with both arms raised;
They contemplate only matters of the past and future, wishing that the Buddha would remain for an eon.
How can I bear to witness today the Parinirvāṇa of the Honored One?
I have constantly wandered seeking the Buddha, yet I do not see the God among Gods;
the Jetavana is now but an empty mound, and I behold only others.
If I enter Vaiśālī, the local elites will inquire after the Buddha’s health.
Born from the Unsurpassed Honored One, how shall I answer?
Thousands of countless people, with tears streaming down their faces, cry out:
"O Lion of the Śākyas, the Unsurpassed One, where has Your Majesty now gone?"
The people wailed and urged him on; there was none who did not long to see the Buddha.
How can you enter the great city and leave the Honored One among Men so far behind?
Upon whom shall we rely hereafter?
For whom shall I carry the alms-bowl?
For whom shall I hold the robes?
Who will personally exhort me?
Who will explain to me what it means to hear and retain?
Who can resolve my doubts, for Ānanda’s knowledge is like the ocean?
From whom did he hear the True Dharma, those profound verses so difficult to understand?
"From whom shall I receive the immeasurable and sublime Dharma?
Then the Buddha told Ānanda:
"For the sake of the Tathāgata, spread a lion's seat between the twin trees."
"Why is this? Because Tāḷaka entered parinirvāṇa at the hour of midnight, in accordance with his original vow.

Thereupon, Ānanda rose from his seat weeping, prepared a lion-seat beneath the twin śāla trees in the Malla territory with its head pointing north, and having finished arranging it, he spoke these verses:
"Now that you, the Great One of Supernatural Powers, have spread this final bed,
I shall never again be able to find such a pure seat.
How could I bear to enter between these twin trees?"
"The Radiant One has now entered parinirvāṇa, Far removed from the Most Honored One.
Thereupon, Anuruddha spoke a verse for Ānanda, saying:
"From the very beginning, the Buddha has taught That all things are entirely impermanent."
"Alone and unable to attain mastery, why do you weep here?
At that time, Ānanda answered Aniruddha in verse:
"How can you speak such words? You should instead answer my question."
"Seeing the Honored One enter parinirvāṇa, how could you, O Benevolent One, be without sorrow?
Thereupon, Anuruddha replied to Ānanda in verse:
"When I see people in distress and peril, my heart is always accompanied by grief and affliction."
My tears flow until my eyes are full, and my sorrowful weeping streams down in torrents.
I too have observed the devas and humans, and with my divine eye I weep;
for this reason as well, I cry out in grief, filled with loathing and bitter anguish.
"Because there is no need for weeping, you shall surely attain what is to be gained;
therefore, I exhort you: do not weep, nor grieve. **Chapter Two:

The Manifestation of Birth of the Four Youthful Disciples** At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and entered between the twin trees. Having entered, he lay down on his right side upon the lion-bed.
At that time, one hundred billion Buddha-lands to the east of here, there was a Buddha named Siṃhaghoṣakṛta Tathāgata, who currently resides and teaches the Dharma.
That world is named Muktapuṣpa.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"For what reason is that world named 'Flowers of Liberation'?

It is because the ground is constantly covered everywhere with flowers made of the seven treasures, leaving no empty space; those flowers are soft, their colors are exceedingly bright and beautiful, and they emit every kind of fragrance."
There were trees made of the seven treasures, composed of various jewels;
there were sandalwood trees adorned with all kinds of sandalwood, their colors exquisite and of countless varieties;
there were trees that constantly produced the sounds of music, the rhythms and melodies being harmonious, elegant, and infinitely well-tuned.
There are trees that constantly produce vessels made of the seven treasures, complete with every variety;
there are trees that constantly produce immeasurable ornaments of various precious necklaces.

That land has countless jewel gardens, formed from the intermingling of many kinds of the seven treasures, like the palaces where the gods dwell, adorned with various *cintāmaṇi* heavenly jewels and polished purple-gold, resembling the palaces inhabited on the sixth heaven.

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are born in that buddha-field all distance themselves from worldly assemblies and exclusively honor the exposition of the Dharma. Possessing the great sages’ supernormal powers, they transcend the infinite; they have attained the lofty and brilliant wisdom of all buddhas. They are able to answer whatever is questioned and remain detached from the world. In their speech and thoughts, they always resolve upon matters of the Dharma. Through skillful means, they manifest inner illumination; they distance themselves from flattery and gain detachment from the assembly of dharmas. Free from all conceptualizations, they attain the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).

Having crossed to the other shore, they are fully endowed with the training in skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); they constantly serve all Buddhas, remain free from worldly discourse, and speak only of the dharmic activities of non-regressive bodhisattvas.

These bodhisattvas take no pleasure in other discourses, but rather deliberate upon the threefold purity of the bodhisattva dhāraṇī-vajra-practice, as well as the Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses; for this reason, that realm is named "Flower of Liberation."
There was a bodhisattva named Kalyāṇārthacintin who suddenly passed away and was reborn in Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, as the son of King Ajātaśatru.
As soon as he was born, he sat cross-legged and spoke these verses:
"The reason I have come from the Lion’s Roar Buddha-field,
Is that I wish to see the Lion of the Śākyas."
"Is the Perfectly Awakened One still present?
Then, another deva spoke this verse for the youth:
"The Honored One among Men today, The Lion of the Śākyas, has laid down his robes."
"Between the twin trees, I shall enter the tranquil state of *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, the youth replied to the deva in verse:
"I have come from the eastern direction, having passed through hundreds of billions of millions of lands."
As for the Lion of the Śākyas, who desires to hear the supreme Dharma— today,
the Honored One among Men shall enter parinirvāṇa in stillness; having reached this place,
I have a karmic affinity with him, for he does not come without such a cause.
Today I have come, for the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa;
In the heavens and throughout the world there shall be sorrow, how much more so for me?
Not remaining still for even the duration of a thought, I wish at once to go and see the Buddha.
"I have come here; my coming has not been in vain, for it is rare for a Buddha to appear in the world.
Thus, I address the Great King:
"Do not be negligent; you should go to the Tathāgata.
Only once in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas does a Buddha arise.
You should know that regarding his virtuous transformation, he does not wrong the common people."
Today, before the Great King, I admonish the honored one of the nation:
because you indulge your whims and follow your desires, how could you sever your father’s life?
You have associated with evil friends; Devadatta is indeed a great thief.
The king followed that instruction and took his father’s life;
arising from the notion of a self, through deluded desire he committed a parricidal offense.
His father had practiced the Dharma and was thus a son of the Buddha.
The King has already incurred this guilt, having committed an act of rebellion;
for this reason, he shall fall into the depths of darkness, into the Avīci hell.
But one whose mind is joyful and who possesses pure faith in the Buddha shall immediately attain liberation.
Thereafter, one becomes honored among men and may attain perfect enlightenment.
Once the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, although one may behold his perfect enlightenment,
one can only offer worship to his selfless relics.
It is not out of desire that I have come to this kingdom;
O Great King, grant me leave to follow my purpose, for I wish to go and see the Buddha.
At this very hour of midnight today, the World-Honored One shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Following the direction of the Lion’s Roar, I have heard the Buddha speak thus;
desiring to see the Buddha, I have therefore come to this Sahā world.
I respectfully bid farewell to my relatives both near and far; may all households remain at peace.
"I shall go to behold the Buddha, whose supernormal powers have brought an end to birth and death;
let those who wish to see the Buddha accompany me as we approach to serve the Honored One at his parinirvāṇa.
Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru addressed his son with these verses:
"Son, you must endure for this night; I shall seek out heroes and go with them in force.
The land of the Mallas is far from here, and it cannot be reached by carriage."
At that time, the youth answered King Ajātaśatru with these verses:
“My power of diligence is exceedingly vast; In the mere instant of a thought, I can arrive here.
This very night, I can transcend incalculable kalpas; I am not indolent, O Great King.”
The distance I have traveled this very day and night is likewise incalculable and exceedingly vast;
having transcended countless kingdoms along the way, what need is there to mention the location of the Mallas?
At that time, the youth descended from his seat and departed on foot from the great city of Rājagṛha, speaking these verses:

“Those who wish to be born in heaven and leave the hells behind, Who desire renown and to become a preeminent hero, Should quickly follow after me; Let us proceed before the Buddha, the Most Nirvāṇa.”

As soon as the youth had left the great city of Rājagṛha and spoken these verses, at that very moment twenty thousand people from within the city, along with countless billions of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, came together to this assembly. Surrounded by such a multitude, they proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, between the twin śāla trees in the birthplace of the Mallas.
At that time, the Buddha was reclining on his right side upon a lion throne.
At that moment, fifty thousand buddha-lands to the south of here, there was a buddha named Ratnākara-vyūha-tathāgata, who was currently residing and preaching the Dharma.
That world is named Ratnabīja.
There was a bodhisattva there named Priyaprasādapariśuddha who suddenly transferred his life-force and was born in the great city of Śrāvastī in Jambudvīpa, becoming the son of the elder Siṃha.
As soon as he was born, he sat cross-legged and spoke this verse:
"For the sake of giving my hands and feet, And even using my ears and nose,
Throughout hundreds of millions of lifetimes, I have endured giving my head as an offering."
Brave in giving, he was without fear, bestowing even his wife, children, and grandchildren;
desiring to deliver all beings, is the World-Honored Śākyamuni not present?
Thus, throughout billions of kalpas, he gave his flesh and muscle to others.
"Out of a desire to deliver sentient beings, is the Eye of the World still present?
Thereupon, the elder Siṃha became so terrified that his hair stood on end, and he questioned his son in verse:
"Are you a deva, a gandharva, a ghost, or a kiṃnara?"
This infant can offer praise, speaking wondrous words with eloquence.
Both those within and without were struck with wonder and fear; both small and great fled in all directions.
Yet, because I heard the voice of the Buddha, I alone did not depart.
At that time, the youth answered his father with a verse:
“I am a deva and also a nāga; I am also a ghost and a kiṃnara.
I am a deva among devas, And also a human householder.”
Thereupon, the elder Siṃha addressed his son in verse:
"Because of hearing these words, my son, you only increase my doubt;
that which you thus extol makes me grow ever more fearful."
What are devas and nāgas?
What are ghosts and gandharvas?
And what is meant by the "God among Gods"?
"What do you mean by 'a son of man'?
At that time, the youth answered his father in verse:
"In the south there is a Buddha named Ratnākara, the Honored Tathāgata."
I have come from that realm and have now arrived at this Buddha-field.
To those who are wrathful and harmful, I appear as Śakra; likewise for the gods of the six heavens.
To those in suffering, I appear as Brahmā, and I also manifest as a Cakravartin king.
Whether they be dragons or elephant-like beings, Or spirits who have come here,
Ghosts, *kumbhāṇḍas*, or *gandharvas*— Householder,
you should understand this. For the sake of all, I shall compassionately provide protection.
Having attained the status of one honored by devas and humans, awakening constitutes the supreme deliverance.
My transformation of others has also been long, continuing from kalpa to hundreds of millions of kalpas;
it shall never come to an end. Elder, I wish now to depart.
The youth said to his father:

"One should study what the Tathāgata Ratnākara has manifested and taught; one should not practice the affairs of the sense bases (*āyatana*). What is cultivated should be the mindful performance of vast deeds."
There are three practices of the bodhisattva by which one quickly attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path of *avaivartika*. What are these three?

First, various profound awakenings; second, entering into countless states of mind; third, the samādhi of mindfulness of essential phrases. These are the three practices by which a bodhisattva quickly attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path of *avaivartika*.
Then the elder Siṃha said to his son,
"I do not yet know that place.
The youth spoke in verse to reveal its location:
"Profound wisdom is difficult to comprehend and difficult to understand; the entire world harbors doubts regarding this teaching.
He who fully understands its meaning is none other than the Buddha, the Tathāgata."
The phrases understood by the Buddha are free from blemish; having attained the state of non-conception is the supreme wisdom.
That path of purity is free from thought and recollection; not engaging in conceptual activity—this is called wisdom.
The infinite mind has no fixed mind; that which the heart enters is the tranquil resolve.
That which has no entry is called "mind"; this mind then perceives all things.
Through the Vajra-samādhi, one attains supreme awakening; herein, there is no phrase that enters into phrases.
I abide in the wondrous Vajra of faith; this track of phrases is called the supreme vehicle.
Those who have severed what is essential do not rely on faith; the Buddha praised the Dharma of faith as the supreme sustenance.
All phenomena are like space; by practicing samādhi, one attains Buddhahood.
There is no wisdom regarding all that is known; there is no practice regarding all that is enacted;
there is no learning regarding all that is studied; there is no speaking regarding all that is spoken.
One who has deeply entered wisdom has no perception of dharmas; Entering into tranquil concentration, there is no perception of tranquility;
Though having realized the path of awakening, there is no perception of awakening; Delivering sentient beings, there is no perception of a person.

This valorous one is free from the net of views; having fully awakened to and realized the profound matters of the Way, he enters the ocean of all birth and death to deliver all sentient beings from their cycles of arising and ceasing.

When the youth had spoken these verses, the elder Siṃha and his two hundred followers fully resolved their minds toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, and they immediately attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Eight hundred million devas conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, immediately establishing themselves on the stage of non-retrogression and attaining unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Four nayutas of people were distanced from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the youth spoke in verse:
"I have not come here in vain; I have exhorted the Śākya Sage to deliver beings beyond measure, Causing them to resolve upon the path of the Buddha."
Within the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas, he embraced and proclaimed the meaning of the good;
he established people on the ground of patience, so that none could fall back.
I established my father, brothers, and all the families upon the Buddha-way.
Eight hundred million devas and humans, all were exhorted toward the Mahāyāna.
For the sake of all people, I have removed their conduct of poverty;
for me, the benefit of attaining the Dharma is incalculable and inconceivable.

When the youth had spoken these verses, he, together with his parents and hundreds of thousands of billions of people, surrounded by countless billions of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas and their retinues, proceeded to the birthplace of the Mallas and approached the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Buddha was reclining on his right side upon a lion throne.
At that moment, eighty billion buddha-fields to the west of here had a buddha named Sukhāvatī Tathāgata, who was currently residing there, preaching the Dharma.
That world was named Garden of Delight (Lian-yuan).

There was a bodhisattva there named Emptiness and Non-existence (Kong-wu) who suddenly transferred his life-force and was born in Jambudvīpa, becoming the son of the elder Susukha in the city of Vārāṇasī.
As soon as he was born, he sat cross-legged and spoke this verse:
“The Dharma is fundamentally empty and non-existent; To desire existence is to be attached.
One cannot escape diligent suffering, And remains forever established in turmoil.”
The Dharma is unattainable; this is called the state of stillness.
It is both exhausted and inexhaustible, for it is entirely non-existent.
One who is empty does not practice with wisdom, nor is there any practice that is not present.
If there were no causes or conditions for him, from what could there be an object of perception?
The Dharma he taught is profound, tranquil, and difficult to understand.
Does the Lion of the Śākyas, the Honored One among men, the Perfectly Awakened One, still exist?
The Great Lion lets out a thunderous roar; his Brahma-voice is without arising or ceasing.
Today, amidst the trees, the light of the sun has set and no longer appears.
The Buddha stands among the assembly of monks like the full moon at its zenith.
People no longer behold the Hero of the World preaching the Dharma.
Amidst the assembly of monks, the Buddha sits as if upon the summit of Mount Sumeru;
the World-Honored One no longer delights in entering or departing from the city.
Roaring the Way for the sake of the world of devas, he preaches the Dharma of emptiness and non-self;
nothing more can be obtained, yet all hear and submit to his great voice.
Departing from "I" and "mine," he extols and proclaims the Dharma of emptiness.
"Now the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, resting in sickness among the trees.
When the youth had spoken this verse, at that very moment, one hundred thousand people in the great city of Vārāṇasī simultaneously raised their voices and praised him together, saying:
"This is unprecedented!

This young boy possesses such profound wisdom-intent, wisdom-entry, radiance of wisdom, purity of wisdom, and loftiness of wisdom; he speaks sublime verses and, from birth, has attained patience, directed wisdom, and skillful means—qualities difficult to reach and unprecedented. Though his body is not yet fully grown, he possesses great power.
"Just as one sees the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment with one's own eyes, may our wisdom be likewise. The youth said:
"O virtuous ones! You should truly aspire for this wisdom;

you should aspire for wisdom such as that of the Buddha—subtle and wondrous, beyond conjunction, tranquil and peerless, free from all that exists, lofty and unimpaired, which brings to fulfillment all dharmas of practice and all roots of goodness."
All Buddhas, by means of their powers and fearlessnesses, abide in great kindness and great compassion.
O virtuous ones!
You should aspire to attain this wisdom.
"I shall now, together with you, resolve upon the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

At that moment, the great assembly all simultaneously resolved upon the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; he then preached the Dharma for them, and they all established themselves in non-retrogression, attaining unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
“Since you all have already resolved upon the Great Way, you may now go together to see the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Thereupon, the youth, together with his parents and one hundred thousand people, surrounded by an incalculable number of billions of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas and their retinues, arrived at the birthplace of the Mallas and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Buddha was reclining on his right side upon the lion throne.
At that moment, sixty-four trillion buddha-lands to the north of here had a buddha named Jueji (Vajrapada) Tathāgata, who currently resides there preaching the Dharma.
That world is named Flower Trace (*Puṣpadarśana*).
In that realm, as well as upon its trees, flowers, and fruits, there constantly resounds throughout day and night the sound of the awakening-flower practices.
All devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas who hear this sound shall all establish themselves in the path of practice at the trace of awakening.
That Tathāgata possesses such virtues that anyone who beholds the radiance of his awakened traces and conduct shall all attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
This is brought about by the power of that Tathāgata’s original vow.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"In the world of Flower Traces of the Tathāgata Awakening Traces, there are none who seek the two vehicles; nor does he teach others to seek them, nor does he provide for his disciples the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. They study only the Mahāyāna and likewise instruct and exhort others to do so."
The Buddha said:

"Since the Tathāgata Jueji (Vijñapti) attained Buddhahood sixty-four hundred thousand kalpas ago, he has had no assembly of disciples or pratyekabuddhas; there has been only an assembly of bodhisattvas."
For example, a Wheel-Turning Sage King has many sons, whom he appoints as ministers, gatekeepers, and attendants.
The realm of the Tathāgata Jueji (Traces of Awakening) is likewise: it relies solely upon bodhisattvas as its assistants, bodhisattvas as its leaders, and bodhisattvas as its treasures.
For this reason, the bodhisattvas in that buddha-field are fully present and complete, constituting the realm of a Buddha. Ānanda!

All that is abundant, flourishing, peaceful, and blissful in the world of the Tathāgata Jñānakrama is crowded with bodhisattvas; it is everywhere pure, and there is not one among them who does not possess supernormal powers.

Taking all vajras as one's wealth, one unites with whatever is heard without doubt or fetters; all that is heard in the assembly is applied to diligent practice, and through the union of the Dharma-mind, one exerts oneself in all practices, striving to cultivate meditative concentration and all noble trainings, accumulating the essential gateways of dhāraṇī within the equanimity of wisdom.
There was a bodhisattva named Ṛddhipuṣpa who suddenly transferred his life-force and was reborn in the great city of Vaiśālī in Jambudvīpa, becoming the son of Siṃha, the minister of war.
As soon as he was born, he sat cross-legged and spoke this verse:
"Among the Śākyas, the Honored One of the Śākyas, Who well expounds the sublime and wondrous Dharma,
Delivering and liberating billions upon billions of people— Does the Perfectly Awakened One still exist?"
The Dharma arises following from intention, yet that intention cannot be apprehended;
there is nothing equal to it within the three realms. Is the Perfectly Awakened One present?
There is no World-Honored One and no form; he has no peer among men.
There is none equal to you; is the One with Clear Vision still present?
In the Perfection of Vigor, with a single mind in dhyāna-samādhi, and with wisdom like the ocean—is the Perfectly Awakened One still present?
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Buddhapada manifested as the youth Devaputra and spoke this verse:
“The Perfectly Awakened One shall abide for one eon, And indeed for even more than that number;
Since the Perfectly Awakened One remains hereafter, You may remain and enjoy yourself.”
"Child, for now you shall practice desire; this is the house of a great king.
With drums, music, and clear-stringed melodies, and with flutes played to your heart's content, you shall amuse yourself.
Then the child, with a celestial mind, spoke a verse in reply to the Tathāgata Buddhapada:
"Those who follow their desires are deluded;
they do not understand the Perfectly Awakened One nor the Buddha’s instructions.
Like pigs, horses, and camels, like foxes, wolves, and donkeys,"
These people are addicted to desire; it is not the practice of the Buddha’s sons.
Blind and deaf, they possess no knowledge; mute and unable to speak—these people are addicted to desire; it is not the practice of the Buddha’s sons.
Moths, bees, and flies, as well as horses and cattle, do not know for themselves;
such beings are addicted to desire, and this is not the conduct of a son of the Buddha.
Even if the land of Jambudvīpa were filled to the brim with fire, [one would rather enter it than follow such ways].
It would be better to fall into that [hell] than to practice sensual desires.
To take pleasure in desire as supreme—how could one ever practice enough of such desire?
To praise desire is to be ignorant of the Dharma.
Because I was not free from desire, my perception was obscured;
when the Buddha came to question me in his transformation-body, I took him to be a deva.
From the Buddha I have heard what the Dharma King has taught regarding the vision of reality as it is.
At this very midnight, the World-Honored One shall enter *nirvāṇa*.
I shall go to see the Buddha, whose supernormal powers are without arising or ceasing.
If you wish to go, let us go together to the place where the Honored One enters *nirvāṇa*.
The Awakened One, the God among Gods, the Honored One among Men, has thus spoken:
one attains the perfection of skillful deliverance, guiding and governing people with light.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the meritorious deeds one has established—
It is not as it was when the World-Honored One, who compassionately covers all, delivered us; he was the protector of this world.
Now that the Buddha is about to enter *nirvāṇa*, sentient beings will again suffer in toil and hardship.
The Buddha is the eye of all; today he shall enter *nirvāṇa*.
This world shall encounter further adversity, falling into great darkness.
The King of Physicians, who extinguishes all maladies, today shall enter *nirvāṇa*.
Now that the Honored One among Men has passed away, the world is filled with profound suffering.
He who could sever all doubts is today about to enter *nirvāṇa*;
those in this world who harbor uncertainty shall once again be consumed by a blazing fire.
The Buddha has eliminated lust, anger, and delusion; today he shall enter Nirvana.
This world shall once again witness the blazing flare-up of the three fires.
Honored by all, revered by gods and men—
"Now, having passed away within these trees, the multitude shall never see him again.
Chapter Three: The Four Boys. At that time, the Buddha lay reclining on his right side upon the lion throne.
At that time, four youths from the four quarters—adorned with great merit—moved by spiritual resonance, went to where the Buddha was.

To whatever prefectures, kingdoms, cities, towns, or villages these four youths traveled, all the people, whether far or near, bowed in reverence and gazed up at them, all of whom cherished them with joy.

As these four youths were walking, the hosts of devas from the heavens came from the four directions, raining down celestial flowers that completely covered the ground, while in the void of space, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayas of musical instruments were played.
At that time, the Buddha manifested four lion seats in the four directions. Then Ānanda, seeing this great transformation and its various forms, asked the Buddha in verse:
"O Light of the World, who has laid out these lion seats to the right in these four directions?"
I pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me:
O Light of the World, who is it that here, from the four directions,
causes all the earth, the famous mountains, and the great oceans to tremble?
The light of the world—who among these four directions has come as a youth?
Who is the one clad in the great armor of saṃnāha?
The light of the world—who among these four quarters [is he]?
Just as at the hour of midnight, the moon rises and displays its brilliance;
who is it that brings light to the world, causing all people and things in the four directions to stir,
and the waves of the rivers and streams to surge?
O Light of the World, who is it that here in the four directions follows behind all these youths amidst every sound?
O Light of the World, who is it that is accompanied by the devas?
"Just as the sun and moon abide, dwelling within the void of space.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see those four youths coming from the four directions?"

His majestic radiance was like that of a celestial countenance, exquisitely wonderful; his divine brilliance was so radiant and upright that it was immeasurable. His conduct was complete, and he possessed the four kinds of Brahma-voices. He entered deeply into the meaning of giving, possessing a sense of shame and auspiciousness; he was always self-reproachful and self-exhorting to achieve perfection, and wherever he went, he invariably delivered sentient beings.

Possessing the eye of wisdom and discernment, endowed with majestic spiritual power and virtue, and possessing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom—the various perfections (pāramitās) and supernormal powers—all give rise to the meaning of all precepts, wholesome dharmas, and principles.
It is like the udumbara flower, which is difficult to encounter and difficult to see even in hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas.

Having practiced the deeds of countless Buddhas and planted the roots of merit under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Buddhas, they have each come from the heavens of various different Buddha-lands in the four directions to be born here in Jambudvīpa, hearing that my body shall enter parinirvāṇa and desiring to witness my parinirvāṇa.
"Tonight at midnight, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa in the birthplace of the Mallas; he is certain to enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see this youth coming from the east?"

With a countenance gentle and refined, and an appearance serene and wondrous, he was surrounded by a retinue of countless billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands; honored by billions of devas with celestial flowers and music, he approached the Tathāgata.

Ānanda! This youth came from the land of the Tathāgata Siṃhanāda; he has constantly been a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) in that land, ruling over a thousand worlds and preaching the Dharma for all devas and humans. By means of his supernormal powers, wisdom, and the knowledge of the noble ones, he travels back and forth without interruption.

He governed the kingdom for eighteen billion years, and during those eighteen billion years, he instructed eighteen *koṭi-nayuta* of bodhisattvas, causing them to first resolve their minds on enlightenment, establish the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and at that very time renounce their homes to practice the study.

For eighty-one billion years he constantly cultivated the pure conduct of Brahma; for eighty-one billion years he never knew how to sit; for eighty-one billion years he never slept or lay down, never thought of desire, never thought of contentious speech, and never thought of harming others. Furthermore, he had no perception of desire, no perception of objects, and no perception of harm; he had no perception of earth, water, fire, or wind; he had no perception of speech and no perception of space; he had no perception of male and no perception of female; he had no perception of hunger and no perception of thirst; he had no perception of trees, no perception of self, and no perception of "self" or "person"; he had no perception of cities or walls, and no perception of arising or ceasing.

Why is this? It is because these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained the samādhi of the extinction of all perceptions, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they have attained the samādhi of non-arising activity and the samādhi of non-extinction; they have attained all bodhisattva samādhis and the samādhi that transcends all dhāraṇī-gates; they have attained all skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), the perfection of supernatural powers and wisdom (*abhijñā-prajñā-pāramitā*), and the practice of the great loving-kindness and compassion of all bodhisattvas.

Turning the wheel of Dharma in all worlds, establishing all people in the state of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, may you turn the wheel of non-retrogression; thus, through great compassion for all, may you bring peace and security to everyone.
The virtues of the youth are thus fully endowed beyond measure; furthermore, through diligence, he practices two superior dharmas. What are these two?
He is detached from the fleshly eye, yet even in that detachment there is no notion of detachment; he speaks within the assembly of the Dharma, yet in that speaking there is no notion of speaking.
Such as these, he never uttered any extraneous words, but chanted only the chapters on the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.

For eighty billion years, he instructed eighty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas, establishing them in the unsurpassed, right, and true path; all of them, having first resolved their minds, were established in the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, eighty-one billion nayutas of bodhisattvas each departed for the Buddha-lands of other directions where the Gods among Gods resided.

All these Buddhas were of one and the same kind; on this very day at midnight, they simultaneously lay down on their right sides upon lion-thrones. All these World-Honored Ones were named Śākyamuni, and all had become Buddhas in the evil world of the five turbidities.
These Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, shall this very day at midnight all enter parinirvāṇa between the twin trees in the birthplace of the Mallas.
Ānanda! The Tathāgata knows all and sees all; he does not see with the fleshly eye.
Furthermore, it surpasses the vision of those who are infinite in number; it is not merely that all disciples and pratyekabuddhas cannot equal it. Ānanda!

If a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, upāsikā, or any among devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans, upon hearing this sutra-dharma, feels joy and faith for even a single moment of thought, they will surpass one who makes offerings to nayutas of Buddhas throughout the course of nayutas of kalpas.
Ānanda! Such is the wisdom and intention of this youth.

Today, within my Dharma, the number of wriggling creatures he has awakened and delivered in a single night surpasses all that Śāriputra and all my other disciples have taught since the beginning of time; even if they were to preach for the duration of an eon, they could not equal it.
"The merit of this youth for delivering sentient beings is thus immeasurable.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see this youth coming from the south?"
It is like the light of the summer sun shining upon the water, or like the full moon possessing abundant radiance.
It is like holding a precious staff and striking the earth until a great sound issues forth— just as a skilled craftsman fashions a bowl of gold or silver,
its form perfectly round and flawless, free from all impurities and endowed with five qualities.
The sound of footsteps; the sound of the ten categories of causes and conditions; the sound of being free from the sixty-two defilements;
the sound of the one hundred and one qualities being fully possessed; the sound of the fifty kinds of perfection; the sound of the ten categories of perfected hands;
the sound of the ten categories of pure eyes; the sound of practicing the sixteen virtues; the sound of the eight classes of beings being fully possessed; and the twelve matters.
The voice endowed with all qualities; the pure voice of a thousand varieties of gold and silver; the superior voice that arises immediately upon being heard;
the golden-colored voice born of tranquility; the voice free from all defects; the voice produced by incense;
the voice that extensively produces what is done; the pure and subtle voice of the six classes of men; and the voice whose lineage is complete.
Fifth, the fifty million sounds of gentle resonance: the sound that brings the thought of peace and removes diligent suffering;
the sound that brings the thought of joy through mindfulness of the Tathāgata; the sound that subdues the power of Māra; the sound that destroys the net of false views;

the sound that extinguishes all afflictions (*kleśa*); the sound that inspires exultation through the thought of the Buddha; the sound that establishes the thought of the peace of non-arising; and the sound of non-retrogression.
The sound of the Wheel of Dharma, the sound of peace, tranquility, and awakening, the sound of the samādhi and samāpatti of the single-minded dharma-gate,
the sound of the ten powers and fearlessnesses, the sound of great kindness and great compassion, and the sound of the ten directions emerging—
these various sounds issued forth as the precious staff struck the earth.
“Ānanda! Fifty hundred thousand Buddha-lands to the south of here, there is a Buddha named Ratnakūṭadarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently residing and preaching the Dharma.”
That world is named Ratnagarbha.

It is called Ratnagarbha because that land is free from all heterodox and deviant paths; it is a realm of true persons who have all earnestly resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment. In that land, even the names of defilements and worldly afflictions are unheard of, nor are the names of the three thoughts—namely, the thoughts of lust, anger, and delusion—ever heard. Furthermore, there is no perception of male or female.
Why is this? Because all practice the pure Brahma-faring.
In that land, one does not nourish the body with solid food; those people have only two kinds of sustenance.
What are these two?
They delight in preaching all-knowledge as their sustenance;
they do not preach the two vehicles of the disciples and the pratyekabuddhas, but preach only the matters of all-knowledge.
Thus, for those bodhisattvas who practice this single path of the Dharma-section, the devas and humans also recite these matters.
Ānanda! That world is therefore named Jewel Seed (Ratnaviśeṣa).

If Bodhisattvas from other worlds are born in that Buddha-land, as soon as they are born, they immediately establish themselves on the stage of non-retrogression and in the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path. They see countless nayutas of Bodhisattvas expounding all matters concerning the Tathāgata and extensively discussing the Dharma-phrases of Bodhisattvas. As soon as they are born in any Buddha-land, they all hear it said: "Today, such-and-such a Bodhisattva has been born in this Buddha-land."

Ānanda! Even if I were to spend one eon, or hundreds of millions of nayutas of eons, speaking of the merits practiced by each and every person in the world-system Ratnakara, I would not yet have finished; nor could they ever be fully exhausted through metaphorical description. I have merely given you a rough account of the virtues of the world-system Ratnakara.

The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana-viśuddha, having manifested such a divine transformation, was born in the land of Jambudvīpa. He came because he wished to witness my parinirvāṇa, and also because he desired to praise the merits of his own land and proclaim the name of that Buddha for the sake of those seeking the bodhisattva path; yet, he observed his own mind to be free from conceptualization.
Ānanda! This Bodhisattva Priyasaddhaśuddha, when he was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, was a universal monarch named Jitaśatru during the time of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.

From sunrise until the time for the morning meal, he bestowed teachings and delivered thirty-six billion bodhisattvas, causing them all to resolve their minds and establish themselves in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

After his parinirvāṇa as a *tīrthakara*, he shaved off his beard and hair and remained complete [in his vows] for a thousand years, turning the wheel of Dharma and delivering countless people. Then, when the sun was about to set, he guided sixty billion bodhisattvas, causing them to first resolve their minds and establish themselves in the patience of non-arising; at that very moment, he caused seventy *nayuta* of people to reach the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) and the liberation of mind.
Ānanda! Such is the beneficial meaning of the *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
If I were to describe to you the merits of the Bodhisattva Hsixinjing (Joyful Faith Purity), even after hundreds of millions of kalpas they would not yet be exhausted.
"Spread a seat for the Bodhisattva Priyadarśanaśraddhāviśuddha before me. Why is this?

This youth has long practiced the Way and his mind never tires or grows weary; those who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Priyadarśanaśraddhāviśuddha and rejoice are as if they have encountered the era of a Buddha, let alone those who see him face-to-face and leap with joy."

Ānanda! Should there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans who, upon hearing this sutra, are able to give rise to even a single thought of reverent acceptance and joy, the Tathāgata beholds all such persons.
I have already foretold that all these individuals shall behold the Tathāgata Jewel-Lineage Manifestation and the bodhisattvas of the world-system Jewel-Lineage.
Ānanda! Hold this sutra in silence; do not transmit it recklessly or lightly.
"Why is this? It is because the people of Jambudvīpa have never heard this sutra, nor have they yet mastered the boundless Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Do you not see this youth coming from the west?

He dances his two feet and shakes his body, causing the earth to tremble violently in two ways; those who see him are struck with awe, their hair standing on end. He subdues all heterodox outsiders and drives away all the hosts of Māras; he destroys all past views, brings peace to all, and removes all suffering. He causes all to rejoice, eliminates the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, delivers all beings to return to the good paths, and saves sentient beings with a great voice.”
“Furthermore, do you see the great fragrant canopy of interlaced jewels coming from the west?
“Indeed, O God among Gods!
I have seen it.”
“Ānanda! As for this fragrant lattice coming from the west, it is called the fragrance that guides and leads all bodhisattvas.
Have you not also heard a great sound emerging from the west?”
“The sound of emptiness, the sound of light, the sound of tranquil concentration, and the sound of the Buddha.
“Yes, O God among Gods! I have heard them.”

“Ānanda! These four great sounds that have issued forth are produced from the pores of the body of the Bodhisattva Emptiness-Non-existence (*Kongwu*). These four great sounds are soft, pleasing, subtle, and flawless;

when these sounds issue forth, they cause sixty-eight *koṭi-nayuta* hundreds of thousands of people to exhaust their outflows and attain liberation of mind, sixty-eight *koṭi-nayuta* hundreds of thousands of people to establish themselves in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), nine hundred million people to establish themselves on the stage of non-retrogression for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and cause two *nayuta* of devas in each of the Buddha-fields to become free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.”
Ānanda! To the west, eighty billion Buddha-fields away from here, there is a Buddha named Sukhāvatī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently dwelling and preaching the Dharma.
That world is named Rāmaṇīyaka. Ānanda! That world is called Rāmaṇīyaka because all therein take delight in the Buddha-dharma;

its precious jewels provide people with pure radiance; it is the dwelling place of non-retrogressive Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas; there are countless pure Bodhisattvas, and no followers of the two vehicles—the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—exist there. They study only the vehicle of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-yāna*) and practice only the path of the Buddhas. All the devas establish themselves in omniscience; they attain a voice of tranquil certainty, understand the coming and going within the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and make offerings to the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, with ten thousand kinds of objects. They subdue the various demonic powers and transform those who have fallen into false views; they extinguish all afflictions (*kleśa*) and tear asunder the net of Māra. With their minds set upon the categories of the Dharma, they cause all beings to be established on the stage of non-retrogression.

He does not speak of other teachings, but preaches only the matters of omniscience; he turns the wheel of the Bodhisattva-dharma chapter, transcends the realm of all defilements, is free from demonic activities, harbors no anger in his mind, and practices loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all.

From each and every pore, there issued forth the sounds of these six hundred dharmas of non-retrogression and the meanings of the categories of Bodhisattva teachings. They attained the three gates of liberation, surpassing the states of the disciples and pratyekabuddhas; they crossed over the three realms and practiced throughout the entire dharma-realm. Abiding in those worlds, they beheld all Buddhas; they transcended all dhāraṇī gateways, attained the awakened wisdom of all Buddhas, and attained the samādhis of all Bodhisattvas. They were free from all evil cognitions, severed all knots of doubt, attained the wisdom of the body-wisdom of all Buddhas, and attained the perfection of supernatural powers, remaining free from flattery and deceit.
By virtue of this vow, may one further attain the ability to make offerings to all Buddhas,
establish all people in the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and cause those with many aspirations to attain the wisdom of the perfection of non-arising.

In future kalpas, the bodhisattva’s conduct shall be established without flaw; in the mere instant of conceiving the aspiration, he shall appear before all Buddhas, no longer subject to birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, or sorrow.

Having attained quiescence, they manifest through skillful means the thirty-two marks to adorn their physical forms; having attained the Dharma-body, they manifest as ordinary bodies to make offerings to and serve all Buddhas. Their minds leap with joy and delight, their wisdom transcends the infinite, and they take pleasure in this bliss, desiring that others likewise do so.
The practices and aspirations of the bodhisattvas in that world are such as these; therefore, it is named the World of Joyful Gardens (*Ratipriya*).
Furthermore, in that World of Joyful Gardens, there are eight kinds of crossroads and bathing pools made of the seven precious gems, filled within with water of eight flavors.
The bottom of that water is covered with sand made of the seven precious gems. Within it are four kinds of lotuses:
the blue is called *utpala*, the red is called *padma*, the yellow is called *kumuda*, and the white is called *puṇḍarīka*; their radiance and colors are exquisite, possessing countless splendors.

In that land there are eight layers of precious trees: gold trees, silver trees, lapis lazuli trees, crystal trees, musāragalva trees, agate trees, elephant-agate precious trees, auspicious-precious trees, awakening-turning precious trees, śarasa precious trees, emerald precious trees, moonlight precious trees, surpassing-sun-and-moon precious trees, variegated-jade precious trees, āmra-fruit precious trees, kumuda-flavored precious trees, and pearl trees of red, blue, and white hues. There are also red sandalwood, blue sandalwood, yellow sandalwood, grape-wine sandalwood, joyous-assembly-deva sandalwood, flavor-producing sandalwood, and uccala sandalwood trees; as well as honey-scented and black-sublime-scented trees, all of whose roots, trunks, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits flourish in abundance.

There were fruit trees, vessel trees, clothing trees, trees for necklaces and ornaments, and music trees; their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were each in full and flourishing bloom. The fragrance of these trees was exquisitely sweet and pervasive, just like that found in the heavens.
Ānanda! Such is that world:

its latticed pavilions are made of gold, which produce soft and gentle sounds; furthermore, its countless other merits also produce soft and gentle sounds. For this reason, that world is named "Garden of Delight."
The Bodhisattva Kungwu (Emptiness-Nonexistent) has come to be born here in this Jambudvīpa through his spiritual transformations, desiring to witness my parinirvāṇa.
Immediately upon birth, he has delivered countless people, performing the work of a Buddha by turning the wheel of Dharma.
"Since countless kalpas past, from every hair-pore of the body of the Bodhisattva Kṣemadatta, these four great sounds have issued forth— gentle, pleasing,
subtle, and flawless. The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
In a past age, there was a Buddha named Vimalanetra.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Prajñārāma.

From the Buddha, that bhikṣu heard the meanings of the four great sounds: countless phrases of wisdom, phrases of diligent effort, phrases of various places, phrases of the eye, phrases of the heavens, phrases of sound, phrases of faith, phrases of the Buddha, phrases of the Dharma, phrases of the Saṃgha, phrases of the lion, phrases of the vajra, phrases of delighting in wisdom, phrases of causes and conditions, phrases of guidance, phrases of distant manifestation, phrases of the truth of suffering, phrases of the origin of suffering, phrases of the cessation of suffering, and phrases of the path leading to its cessation.

For seven nights, he constantly maintained mindfulness without departing from these phrases; distancing himself from other discourses, he contemplated the four meanings in his mind—neither abandoning anything nor giving rise to anything—purifying his resolve and contemplation to destroy all views.

Having received these four great sets of countless meaningful phrases from billions of Buddhas, he dwelt in the exposition of the Dharma; for six years, he traveled among the various provinces, kingdoms, districts, and villages to the homes of people, preaching the Dharma within the assemblies and delivering countless beings.
Ānanda! At that time, there was a māra named Kiṭa who manifested as a dragon-elephant with an incalculable host. He rained down molten vajras upon this bhikṣu’s body, causing him to pass away.
Ānanda! That bhikṣu Prajñārāma was none other than the bodhisattva Śūnyatā.

Because he employed his diligence and great wisdom to preach the Dharma within the assemblies for six years, from countless kalpas ago his pores have emitted these four kinds of subtle, flawless, soft, and pleasing sounds; with each single pore, he has delivered countless beings.

For those people of Jambudvīpa who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Emptiness-Non-existence (Śūnyatā-abhāva), it is a source of great benefit and auspicious celebration; how much more so for those who behold him face-to-face with joy.
Having attained countless *pāramitās*, the Bodhisattva Emptiness-Non-existence has come desiring to see the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
“Ānanda! You shall spread a seat for the Bodhisattva Emptiness (Śūnyatā) before me; from this, you shall attain the honor of Great Wisdom.
Thereupon, Ānanda received these instructions and immediately spread a seat for the Bodhisattva Emptiness before the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Because you have prepared this seat, after my parinirvāṇa, you shall attain the six supernormal powers with a single-minded focus while seated upon it.

If you do not set your will on manifesting pure conduct, the merit of preparing this seat will allow you to become a wheel-turning sage-king as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; for each time you become such a king, you shall behold a Buddha and attain the state of unsurpassed, perfect, true, and complete enlightenment."

Should there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, or any other sentient beings with breath and movement who hear this Great Pure Dharma—whether they see the Tathāgata present today or after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa—and prepare a seat for the bhikṣu who is a Dharma-preacher, by the mere act of preparing it, they shall obtain the merit of ten seats.
What are the ten?
First, the seat of the Venerable One;
second, the seat of the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin).
Third, the Śakra-seat;
fourth, the Brahmā-seat;
fifth, the seat of the sixth heaven;
Sixth, the seat of a Dharma-preaching bhikṣu;
seventh, wherever one sits, one shall obtain the Dharma-seat;
eighth, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva approaches the foot of the Bodhi tree, he shall obtain the Buddha-seat.
Ninth, he attains the seat from which the turning of the wheel of Dharma is heard throughout all worlds, delivering countless billions of devas and humans;
tenth, when he enters parinirvāṇa in this manner, surrounded by a retinue of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, he then attains the Tathāgata’s lion throne.
These are the ten.
Ānanda! For the sake of the Bodhisattva Kṣāntivādin, join your ten fingers together and recite these verses:
"His detachment from the sense-faculties is tranquil concentration; Emptiness and non-arising are his great radiance.
I, with courageous palms joined, Pay homage with the great roar of a lion."
With single-minded resolve and diligence, Accumulating wisdom until it is complete,
I join my palms in true goodness, And pay homage to the One who has no equal.
Then the Buddha spoke these verses for the sake of the venerable Ānanda:
“O you who are a bodhisattva of emptiness, With single-minded devotion, join your palms;
As for the merit you shall obtain, Listen now to what I say.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"By the merit of this joining of palms, after my parinirvāṇa, during the sixth month you shall become a Buddha alone; all people in the heavens above and on the earth below shall bow their heads and pay homage to you."

Whether you travel on the road through commanderies and kingdoms, or reside in a vihāra, all men, women, boys, and girls; all those of heterodox paths, śramaṇas, and brahmins; kings, ministers, lecture halls, and pavilions; the sounds of drums echoing through mountains and valleys; lions, tigers, wild oxen, elephants, camels, cattle, horses, donkeys, and monkeys; gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and female ghosts; trees with their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, and all medicinal herbs—whether possessing consciousness or lacking it—all shall yield in deference and pay you respectful homage.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“For example, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha attained the gateway to the path of Buddhahood, all the trees and medicinal plants—whether possessing consciousness or lacking it—yielded to one another, bowing and rising as they turned toward the Bodhi tree.”

Ānanda! Whether there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth, or any other sentient beings possessing breath and life, should any among them speak these words of the Great Pure Dharma—whether the Tathāgata is currently present or has entered parinirvāṇa—if they proclaim them with a heart free from flattery and, with single-minded devotion, join their palms toward the speaker of the Dharma, all Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, shall bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment. Even those with but slight merit shall fully attain this Dharma; how much more so those who delight in it and are free from defilement.

What the Buddha speaks is never otherwise. Hearing these words of the Great Pure Dharma, few feel joy and faith, while many do not delight in hearing them. Those who, upon hearing this teaching, believe and rejoice—the Tathāgata has already foreseen and known such persons. They have not planted the roots of virtue under only one Buddha; rather, they have accumulated merit under hundreds of millions of nayutas of Buddhas. All shall witness me preach this Great Parinirvāṇa Assembly, and they shall further make offerings to the Tathāgata Maitreya.

When you see Maitreya Buddha descend to become a Buddha, you shall again hear him preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; you shall again see the Bodhisattva Kūṇi’s body emit sounds from its pores and great voices; you shall again obtain the Vaipulya sūtras; and you shall again hear and see the four youths preaching this sūtra at that time. Devas, humans, asuras, and all people of the world shall again pay respect, yield in courtesy, and perform the *añjali* salutation, and you shall likewise obtain the lion throne.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Aniruddha:
"Do you see those forty billion devas in the midst of the void who, having heard this Dharma of the sutra, join their palms toward me?"
He replied, “Indeed, O God among Gods!
I have seen it.”
The Buddha told Aniruddha:

"These forty billion devas, by virtue of the merit of this act of joining their palms, shall not fall into the three evil realms for asankhyeya kalpas. Each shall become a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) as many times as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River; in each instance of becoming a sage king, they shall constantly encounter and behold a Buddha. After this number of lifetimes has passed, they shall then attain Buddhahood, all bearing the same title: Tathāgata Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha Praṇidhānaśānta."

At that time, within the assembly, there were powerful men: first, Nani; second, Rati; third, Śūradatta; fourth, Camakālu; fifth, Pukhasu; sixth, Bāśuccha; seventh, Abhita; eighth, Vināti; ninth, Uttara; tenth, Bubhūccha; eleventh, Haripura; twelfth, Khaliśa; thirteenth, Khalidhālu; and fourteenth, Camaccha. Each of these powerful men, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, went to where the Buddha was with weeping and lamentation. They prostrated themselves in salutation, their tears falling in profusion, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "O World-Honored One!..."

We, for the sake of the Bodhisattva Emptiness-Non-existence, the Bodhisattva Skillful Contemplation, the Bodhisattva Joyful Faith-Purity, the Bodhisattva Supernatural Flower, as well as the great assembly of Bodhisattvas, this Great Sūtra, and the multitude of great disciples, join our palms, yield with courtesy, and pay respectful homage; we take these merits and seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, the Buddha smiled.
The Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha in verse:
“The Buddha is the light of the world; for what cause and condition do you smile now?”
"Please explain for us, so that the doubts of countless billions of people may be resolved.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses to Ānanda:
"Ānanda, do you see this multitude of Mallas?"
Each with five hundred retinues, have they not resolved their minds upon the Great Way?
For my sake, join your palms in reverence, as well as the youths K'ung-wu and all the other bodhisattvas, toward this honored Dharma of the sutra.
Exhorting others toward the resolve for the Great Way, And taking pity on all beings,
each with a retinue of five hundred, They shall all attain the path of Buddhahood;
For countless billions of kalpas, They shall never again fall into the evil realms.
Behold those who join their palms in reverence; such is the merit they possess.
I could dwell in patience for an eon, or even for hundreds of millions of eons.
When the Buddhas attain the Way, their lands are exceedingly joyful.
Wherever he travels, he is honored; his land becomes prosperous.
I have dwelt in patience for an eon, yet I cannot finish expounding it all.
Ānanda, this very day, at the hour of midnight,
"You shall be the one to deliver the final teaching, seeing the Buddha, the Honored One among Men.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see this youth coming from the north, who comes forth with a great radiance of golden light?"

The majesty of his divine power illuminated the grasses, trees, medicinal herbs, and forests of the northern quarter; the trunks, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the trees, as well as the palaces, latticed pavilions, mountains, hills, streams, and valleys, along with humans and non-humans, all appeared together as golden in color.
He replied, "Indeed it is so, O God among Gods!
I have seen it."
“Ānanda! Do you see the gabled hall made of the seven treasures coming from the north? He replied:
"Yes indeed, O God among Gods! I have seen it. "Ānanda!"
"Do you see the one sitting cross-legged within the golden lattice?
He replied, "Indeed, O God among Gods!"
"I have seen it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Sixty-four hundred million buddha-fields to the north of here, there is a buddha named Jueji (Vijitāvin) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently present and preaching the Dharma."

The Bodhisattva Ṛddhipuṣpa, having manifested such supernatural transformations there, was born here in Jambudvīpa desiring to witness my parinirvāṇa. At that time, he mistook the radiance of light for the majestic spiritual power of a Tathāgata; he mistook the seven-jeweled lattice canopy for the world-system Padmavati; and he mistook the youth seated within the seven-jeweled golden lattice pavilion for a Tathāgata.
He naturally manifested this world and sat within this seven-jeweled golden lattice canopy, causing countless people to become fully endowed with the roots of virtue. Ānanda!
In this Buddha-field, there are countless hundreds of thousands of millions of people who, together with this youth, have planted the roots of all virtues.

As soon as this youth is born into this Buddha-field, he shall cause his entire assembly of peers to exhaust their outflows, achieve liberation of mind, abide on the stage of learning, and attain non-retrogression from the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
