Thereupon, the four bodhisattvas went to where the Buddha was and, arriving at the same time, prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“That which the Tathāgata ought to do, as well as that which his disciples must do, is to cause all beings to fully attain their proper place.”

By means of this transformation of the golden lattice-canopy, the Bodhisattva Viśeṣacintin caused seven billion people to attain arhatship; seven billion nayutas of people to abide in the stage of training (śaikṣa-bhūmi); seven billion hundred people to establish themselves in the unsurpassed, right, and true path; seven billion nayutas of people to attain the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); and countless people to encounter the time of Maitreya.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume One;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Four: Entrustment. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May the World-Honored One remain for one kalpa, and even beyond one kalpa.”
Why is this? O Devātideva!
Because it is only when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, dwells in the world that these noble beings come here, so that we may see them, prostrate before them, and serve them.
"After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, we shall be forever severed from three things.
What are these three?
The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha."
"These true persons have departed from the three states.
When Ānanda had spoken these words, he wept and fell prostrate on the ground.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadramati spoke this verse to Ānanda:
“Ānanda, my friend, do not weep; all things are impermanent.
Where there is meeting, there must be parting—how much more so for human beings?
Since this world is empty and devoid of self, Ānanda, why do you weep?”
All who gather together find that such assemblies are difficult to endure;
even the Way of the Buddha cannot be attained—Ānanda, why do you grieve?
That which is joined is empty, and wisdom itself is likewise empty.
Whether with thought or without thought, all phenomena are without thought.
Unattainable, empty, and non-existent, they are like a mirage,
or like conjured elephants and horses, or like the flowers of trees in a grove.
"Like what is manifested by a skillful illusionist, so it is with the disciples of the Buddha.
Thereupon, Ānanda replied to the Bodhisattva Bhadramatī in verse:
"It is truly as you have said; all phenomena are devoid of conceptualization."
Today I shall depart, far removed from the World-Honored One;
how shall I enter Śrāvastī when questioned? What answer shall I give?
Is the Perfectly Awakened One still present?
Will the Dharma-eye remain in the future?
If one enters Mount Xiangji and does not see the Honored One among Men,
but sees only his empty seat, how could one bear to dwell there?
If one emerges from Mount Xiangji and enters the Kāli Vihāra,
the Honored One among Men is therein, extensively expounding the Four Noble Truths;
yet seeing that the Kāli Grove is empty, there is no divine radiance of the World Hero.
If one enters the Garden of Sounds, one weeps there all alone;
because one does not see the Perfectly Awakened One, one runs toward the four quarters,
eyes filled with tears— how can one endure staying there?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana-viśuddha spoke these verses to the Venerable Ānanda:
"If one were to grieve for hundreds of millions of years, what could possibly be gained thereby?"
Ānanda, observe this: the Dharma-realm is exceedingly difficult to attain.
It is like the plantain tree; if one were to peel away leaf by leaf until nothing remains, there would be nothing to be found. All phenomena are just like this.
Just as when it rains from heaven, bubbles arise within the water and vanish as soon as they appear, so too are all things.
Like the froth upon the water, they can only be beheld with the eye.
That which is obtained cannot be grasped; the fourfold [elements] are likewise so.
Just as a reflection appears in a clear mirror yet cannot be grasped, so too are the three realms; Ānanda, why do you weep?
Thereupon, Ānanda replied to the Bodhisattva Śraddhādhimukta-viśuddha with these verses:
"It is not that I do not know this, nor is it that I do not see this: that the three realms are non-existent. This has been constantly and perpetually proclaimed."
Seeing these hundreds of millions of people, their tears flowing in mutual streams, coming to my presence in sorrowful weeping, I am moved to even greater grief.
Now the World-Honored One is about to depart; the Supreme among Men will suddenly vanish from sight.
Where should I seek it? Who will protect me?
From whom shall I hear the Dharma, those profound and difficult-to-understand verses?
"What difficulty could there be in entering [the path]? Alas! A Buddha is difficult to encounter!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kūṭāgāra spoke this verse to Ānanda:
"Ānanda, arise and do not grieve; contemplate what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma."
Since phenomena are ungraspable, by what cause could there be cessation?
As when the Buddhas were born, so too was their attainment of the Way;
as the Buddhas turned the wheel of Dharma, so too is their parinirvāṇa.
Birth does not arise from birth, and the Buddha-way likewise has no cessation;
regarding this dharma of non-arising, Ānanda, why do you weep?
Behold the pores of my body and all the karmic deeds therein that I have taught.
"It is taught that the Buddha is empty and non-existent; the Dharma-realm is likewise so.
Thereupon, Ānanda replied to the Bodhisattva Śūnyatābhāva in verse:
"May you all depart; have no anxiety regarding any realm."
We behold billions of Buddhas preaching the supreme and wondrous Dharma;
we and billions of devas surround them on every side,
while bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs together raise their voices in sighs of wonder.
Some from as far as thousands of li all come to where I am;
their cries of lamentation are heard afar, reaching wherever the Lion of the Śākyas resides.
From the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens, and from Tuṣita and Nirmāṇarati, [they come].
The World-Honored One has reached the Brahma-world; when will he descend?
Having dwelt in seclusion for three months, with a single-minded heart, O Honored One among Men—O Hero of the World, when will you arise and once again beat the drum of the Dharma?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ṛddhipuṣpa spoke these verses to Ānanda:
"I have already known this; I have set my own expectation for three months.
I have manifested myself before you, O Benevolent One; Ānanda, you should not weep."
I shall now, for your sake, petition the Tathāgata to turn the foremost Dharma, so that you may be separated from the Śākya Sage.
The Buddhas possess great compassion; they will surely come to where you are.
Ānanda, do not grieve, for the Honored One among Men has arisen.
Even the devas and nāgas are filled with sorrow; how much more so for you?
Such radiance as this shall now perish from the world.
"The Buddha has spoken thus; having heard it directly from the World-Honored One, even if one were to remain for a hundred million kalpas, those gathered here would still part.
Thereupon Ānanda rose and stood before the Buddha, raising his voice three times to recite this verse:
“The Buddha is the protector of all; today he shall enter *nirvāṇa*.
The world shall fall back into darkness, as if having lost its clear vision.
Kings and noble lords will be stripped of their kingdoms and endure great suffering.”
How can I bear to hear these words—that the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa?
The Mallas, the Malla wives, and the Malla sons have all come together;
filled with grief, they weep as they behold the World-Honored One for the last time.
The various classes of devas and nāgas, extending for five yojanas in every direction,
had tears flowing down to their knees, with the exception of the other common people.
The nāga Nandopananda was there together with sixty billion nāgas.
All came together to weep, seeing the World-Honored One for the last time.
The nāga Andhavana and the nāga Sāgara, possessing great power,
wept with tears reaching one yojana as they went to the place where the Buddha was.
The Naga King Anavatapta, surrounded by ten billion followers,
with tears and snot flowing like chariot wheels, went to where the Buddha was.
The Naga King Elapatra manifested a massive body and came forth.
Weeping with a loud cry, they went to where the Buddha was.
A thousand billion spirits and hundreds of nayutas of beings came forward,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and for the last time beheld the World-Honored One.
There were billions of Śākyas, their hosts numbering hundreds of nayutas;
they went before him to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet, saying, “O One of Clear Vision, do not enter nirvāṇa!
Then there were billions of Brahmā devas, whose brilliant radiance illuminated this world and the heavens.
Having previously prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he prayed: "May the Honored One remain for an eon.
When the son of Māra arrived there, the Guide himself declared his presence:
"Out of compassion for all beings, may the Honored One remain for an eon."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śūnyatāvacara spoke these verses for the sake of the Śakras, Brahmās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, māraputras, and śāstṛs:
"You all are utterly ignorant, Uttering only words of forceful dharma;
Having already engaged in heedless conduct, Now you finally weep."
Just as when a young elephant, dwelling in ignorance,
is struck with a sword, it immediately cries out in terror and grief;
so too are you all, for everyone is weeping.
If the Perfectly Awakened One were still present, one might still practice heedless conduct;
but today his light shall depart. His wisdom is like the ocean—what will you do?
“The World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the venerable Aniruddha, Mahākātyāyana, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Kumāra-Kāśyapa, Subhūti, Maudgalyāyana, and Mahākauṣṭhila:
“Each of you extend your arms and place them in the Tathāgata’s palm.”
At that moment, one hundred thousand bhikṣus extended their arms to receive the palms of the World-Honored One.
The Buddha took the palms of the bhikṣus with his left hand, while with his right hand he took the palms of Ānanda and Rāhula and placed them within the hands of the bhikṣus, saying:
"The reason I personally honor Ānanda and Rāhula and entrust them to you is this."
At that moment, a great natural voice arose as if from an image, its sound proclaiming throughout an entire Buddha-field.
Upon hearing this exhortation, the thousand bhikṣus wished to cast off their lives and said:
"We shall first enter parinirvāṇa; we cannot bear to witness the time when the Hero of the World enters parinirvāṇa."
Thereupon, the Buddha extended his arm toward the north; at that very moment, five hundred Buddhas from other worlds in the ten directions extended their hands and placed them in the Buddha’s palms.
The Buddha then took the hands of Ānanda and Rāhula and placed them within the palms of those Buddhas, saying:
"I entrust my beloved Ānanda and my son Rāhula to the care of all you World-Heroes."
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
“I entrust my son Rāhula, And my attendant Ānanda,
Face-to-face, I commit them to you, The World-Honored Ones among all Buddhas.”
Who is able to provide protection for those who are without protection?
Only the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, whose wisdom is free from all obstruction.
This night at midnight, among devas, nāgas, and the people of the world—
Those who dwell in Jambudvīpa shall no longer be able to see me.
Surveying all worlds throughout their infinite and inconceivable extent,
not a single person is to be seen who is destined to abide as one delivered.
For incalculable billions of kalpas, like the sands along the banks of the Ganges,
for the sake of even a single person, one may endure through that many kalpas.
Those who revere and honor the Buddha-Dharma— I shall deliver such people according to my purpose.
"Because they lack reverence and diligence, even a hundred million Buddhas cannot heal them.
At that time, each of the five hundred Buddhas desired to return to their own lands; having placed their hands upon the palms of Ānanda and Rāhula, they spoke these verses:
"For those who honor and revere the Buddhas, the Buddhas shall deliver such persons through the meaning of the Dharma."
Manifesting deliverance and liberation, he immediately beats the great drum of the Dharma.
The World-Honored One, the Lion of the Śākyas, washes away all sorrows and afflictions,
satisfying hundreds of millions of people like rain moistening the earth.
Thereupon Ānanda and Rāhula knelt before the Buddhas and, weeping with grief, spoke this verse:
"May all you great heroes Exhort the Honored One to remain for one kalpa;
By the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, May he remain for one kalpa."
"Causing countless billions of people to attain the meaning and abide in the True Truth;
may the devas, nāgas, and all spirits all resolve their minds upon the Great Way.
At that time, after the five hundred Buddhas had each returned to their respective worlds, they addressed the Venerable Ānanda and Rāhula, saying:
"Stop, Ānanda! Stop, Rāhula! Be without sorrow and without lamentation."
The Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, have completed the extension of their arms for the sake of the Dharma.
Whether they emit radiance, arrive, or remain, these are the manifestations of the Buddhas.

5. Chapter on Crossing Over the Hells. At that time, the Buddha entered a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of rays of light from the big toe of his right foot. From the tip of each ray of light, he manifested hundreds of thousands of millions of lotus flowers; upon each lotus flower, he manifested hundreds of thousands of millions of thrones; and upon each throne sat a manifested Tathāgata preaching the Dharma. Each of these Tathāgatas established hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of people in the stage of non-arising and non-extinction.
At that time, the Buddha again emitted hundreds of thousands of nayuta-koṭi rays of light from his big toe of the left foot;
he emitted ten billion nayuta-koṭi rays of light from his ten toes; he emitted ten billion nayuta-koṭi rays of light from his ten fingers;
and he emitted two billion nayuta-koṭi rays of light from his two knees and two billion [rays] from his two kneecaps.

From his crown, he emits hundreds of thousands of *nayuta* of rays of light; from his secret organ hidden like that of a horse (*aśvakośa*), he emits hundreds of thousands of *nayuta* of rays of light;
from the center of his forehead, he emits hundreds of thousands of *nayuta* of rays of light; from his two shoulders and elbows, he emits two hundred million *nayuta* of rays of light;
from the fontanelle (*mūrdhāntara*), he emits hundreds of thousands of *nayuta* of rays of light; and from his left and right flanks, he emits two hundred million [rays of light].
From his forty teeth, he emitted four hundred thousand nayuta-koti rays of light; from his face, he emitted one hundred thousand nayuta-koti rays of light;
from the mark on the crown of his head (uṣṇīṣa), he emitted one hundred thousand nayuta-koti rays of light;
and from his thirty-two marks of a great man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa), he emitted three hundred and twenty billion nayuta-koti rays of light.
From between his two eyebrows, he emitted hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of light rays.

From each of his eighty minor marks, he likewise emitted hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of light rays. At the tip of each light ray, there appeared hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of transformed lotuses; upon each lotus, there were hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of transformed seats; and upon each seat sat a Tathāgata preaching the Dharma.

These Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not discourse on divergent meanings; they only recite the Bodhisattva-dharmaparyāya, the Dhāraṇī, the Vajracaryā, and the three categories of pure power and fearlessness.
Each transformed Tathāgata established hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of people in the stage of non-retrogression.

At that time, the Buddha further manifested a transformation-body Buddha between the twin trees, who went to the great Avīci hell of the former scholars and emitted a radiance; that light shone everywhere throughout the Saṃjīva hell.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"These people have already attained liberation, yet they repeatedly give rise to conceptual thoughts;
because they habitually give rise to such thoughts, they cause themselves to experience suffering and affliction."
In this world there are those who have attained the Way; the Buddha, the World-Honored One, emits radiance.
That which he teaches regarding the True Dharma causes all suffering and affliction to be extinguished.
There is nothing exhausted and nothing to be attained; there is neither arising nor ceasing.
"Whoever understands this Dharma will never again fall into the evil realms.

As soon as the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, at that very moment, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings were liberated from the Saṃjīva Hell and were immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Then the Buddha again went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and repeated these verses:
"These people have already attained liberation, yet they repeatedly give rise to conceptual thoughts;
because of the habituation to such thoughts, they cause suffering to arise within them."
In this world there are those who have attained the Way; the Buddha, the World-Honored One, radiates brilliant light.
That which he has taught regarding the True Dharma causes all suffering and affliction to be extinguished.
There is nothing to be exhausted and nothing to be attained; there is neither cessation nor arising.
"Whoever knows this Dharma will never again fall into the evil realms.
As soon as the World-Honored One had finished speaking these verses, at that very moment, hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of people who heard this Dharma attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Having attained the supernormal powers, he then spoke this verse:
"Without arising and without ceasing, Without birth and without extinction—
Thus have I understood the Dharma, Attaining the nirvana of the path of patience."
His wisdom is like a radiant light, illuminating the fundamental roots of all beings;
manifesting causes and conditions for liberation, he immediately delivers the people therefrom.
Extinguishing sorrow and suffering, he attains great knowledge and heals all humanity.
Healed by all the Buddhas, he shall never again fall into the evil realms.
His great radiance, though swift, will eventually be extinguished within the world;
yet it causes hundreds of millions of people who are being scorched and roasted to attain liberation from the realm of thought-hell.

Thereupon, the Buddha again went to the four great hells of Saṃjīva (Reviving), Kālasūtra (Black Thread), Saṃghāta (Crushing), and Raurava (Crying Out)—where beings are scorched, roasted, boiled, and burned by falling black sand—and bestowed upon them golden light that pervaded all other lights.

The Buddha’s radiance is soft and pleasing; with eyes of compassion, he gazes upon all beings, bestowing his vision so they may find peace, and employing wisdom and precepts to bring them coolness. He creates the light of tranquil concentration, which pervades everywhere within it.

His majestic spiritual power is supreme and pure, untainted by defilements and far removed from all impurity. He bestows the practice of wisdom; with great kindness and great compassion, he grants boundless peace and happiness. He bestows the unobstructed eye of insight; he bestows the fragrance of precepts that illuminates all things. Having bestowed the flavor of the Dharma and attained mastery over all, he manifests the Dharma-body. He bestows the eye of the Dharma-mind, severing the roots of all that is unwholesome and conferring all pure and white dharmas. He utterly destroys the power of Māra and strikes terror into him, causing those of heterodox paths to sever all views, and enabling all beings to attain the perception of peace and security.

Open the Gate of Heaven and block the doors of evil; replace all toil and suffering with inexhaustible virtue; with single-minded diligence, practice compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity; and constantly lead all beings toward the Great Unconditioned.

He bestows his eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind; from all his pores he emits great radiance; he preaches the Dharma with gentle and pleasing words, speaking noble speech with a voice of compassion.
"I have come to bestow peace upon the world; I have come to liberate all from suffering and pain;
for the sake of those who toil, I shall remove their manifold dust of affliction."
The Dharma that I preach illuminates with the pure and peaceful light of the Honored One;
all people who hear this Dharma shall abandon all evil realms.
Whoever takes refuge in the Buddha attains great benefit;
throughout the cycles of birth and death for billions of eons, they shall never fall into the various evil realms.

When the Buddha had spoken these verses, at that very moment, every single one of the great hells was completely emptied of its hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of beings, who were all liberated and reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven; because they had heard this Dharma, they all attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
Having attained the supernormal powers, he then spoke this verse:
"Just as when on a perilous road, there is a wise guide who leads a great caravan of merchants across hostile bandits and malevolent spirits."
The Buddha’s deliverance is thus: taking radiance as the path, he has liberated billions of people, freeing them from calamity, lust, anger, and delusion.
We take refuge in the Buddha; the Guide emits this radiance.
Having already given rise to the mind of compassion, they bring relief to all who suffer;
one should take refuge in the Dharma, which nurtures my very being.
The Sangha is a precious jewel, whose virtue is inconceivable.

At that time, the Buddha went to the Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, and Saṃghāta hells—the three unpleasing hells—and emitted five hundred *koṭi-nayuta* kinds of golden light that illuminated them everywhere. Through the concentration of tranquility, which is without person, without things, and without arising or ceasing; through the *pāramitās* of giving, morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; through great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great protection; through the practice of the four debts of gratitude; through the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; through the Tathāgata’s noble conduct and worldly wisdom; and through the transformations of supernormal power, the transformations of preaching the Dharma, and the transformations of instruction, he employed his great intelligence.
By means of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, samādhis, and samāpattis, employing all the practices of a bodhisattva;

by means of the unimpeded wisdom of a Buddha, the unimpeded Buddha-eye, the unimpeded Dharma-eye, the unimpeded wisdom-eye, the unimpeded divine eye, and the unimpeded flesh-eye; and by means of great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Regarding all applications of the unsurpassed virtues of all Buddha-dharmas, he employs the awakened dharmas of all Tathāgatas.

Therein, those eight hundred million nayuta hundreds of thousands of sentient beings were all graced by five hundred trillion nayuta kinds of light-sounds; they were freed from all toil and suffering and attained peace and security. They emerged from those Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, and Unpleasant Ground hells and were reborn among the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas. Having heard this Dharma, they became resolute and attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
Thereupon the Buddha remained in the Brahma Heaven and spoke these verses:
"When people are free from diligent toil, That is the foremost peace.
To explain what corresponds to diligent toil: All perceptions are without conceptual thought."
When there is no conceptualization of anything at all, as has been explained here,
how could one find peace within the three realms?
There would only be repeated birth and death.
Whoever understands the emptiness of emptiness, for them emptiness is truly empty;
those who speak of deep fetters, they are able to liberate themselves through emptiness.
Emptiness has no arising, and conceptual thought has no boundary.
Having seen that phenomena are not-self, one is then a child of the Buddha.
This dharma is not "mine," nor can a self be found;
for one who is already without a self, what joy could there be?

When the Buddha had spoken these verses, at that very moment, those hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of people who heard the Dharma all severed every defilement within their minds. Their cycle of birth and death having ended, they attained the realization of Arhatship and relinquished their physical lives to enter parinirvāṇa, saying:
"We cannot bear to witness the time when the World-Honored One enters parinirvāṇa."
Chapter Six: Manifesting All Buddhas. At that time, the Buddha suddenly vanished from the Brahma Heaven and immediately took his place between the twin trees.
The Buddha thought to himself: "Tonight at midnight, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa here. This will be the final time for the people to behold the Buddha’s passing.

I shall briefly cause the multitude to rejoice, so that they may attain thoughts of peace and security, sever all defilements and poisons, and bring to mind the Tathāgata as the source of great wholesome roots. May they be freed from the afflictions of the assembly and attain boundless celebration; may they give rise to great kindness and great compassion, cast off all demonic activities, and embrace all Buddha-dharmas. May they tear asunder the net of all views, extinguish all worldly toils, abandon all flattery and deceit, and discard all grandiose views. May they come to the various *pāramitās*, extol the conduct of the Bodhisattvas, manifest all Tathāgatas so that everyone may see them with their own eyes, and perform great transformations while preaching the Buddha-dharma."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One lay on his right side upon the lion throne, like a lion free from fear.
The Great Honored Hero surveyed the ten directions and pressed the earth with his toe, causing the realms of the ten directions to tremble six times.

The Buddha immediately entered the Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Image, and from each and every pore there issued forth rays of light as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; each ray of light illuminated Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and these rays never intermingled with one another.

By means of this number, from each and every pore he emits as many rays of light as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; having emitted them, he immediately enters the samādhi of "Just as It Is" (yathāvat), causing the eyes of all people to regain the Buddha-eye, so that they all see everything within all the Buddha-lands.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Do you see the eastern direction, ten thousand yojanas in length, breadth, and height, filled with dust? The number of Buddhas in the eastern direction is equal to these particles of dust; each particle represents one Buddha, all of whom lie reclining on their right sides."

The manifestations seen are likewise thus: all the Buddhas who have completed their teaching and deliverance have entered between the twin trees at the birthplace of the Malla; they are all named Śākyamuni, and all lie upon lion-thrones, and all shall enter parinirvāṇa this very day at midnight.

Do you see, sirs, the countless, innumerable, inconceivable, and immeasurable bodhisattvas from the eastern direction who, having perfected their practices, proceed to the foot of the Bodhi tree; do you further see those infinite numbers who have attained the Way of the Buddha?
Have you further seen other countless turners of the wheel of Dharma?
Have you further seen other countless preachers of the Dharma?
Have you further seen those who have immeasurably extended their lifespans?
"Furthermore, do you see anyone else reclining on their right side upon a lion throne,
lying just as I am? The assembly replied,
"We have seen them, but we do not know their number."
The Buddha said:
"Suppose, for example, that the great trichiliocosm—from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven above down to the very limits of the earth—were filled with dust."
"What do you think? Is it possible for anyone to know the number of those atoms?
"Certainly not, O God among Gods!"
"It is incalculable, immeasurable, incomparable, and innumerable.
The Buddha said:

“Suppose there were as many hundreds of thousands of billions of trichiliocosm worlds as there are in this trichiliocosm, and it were filled with dust particles; suppose there were Buddha-lands in the eastern direction equal in number to those dust particles, where Bodhisattvas named Śākyamuni attained the Way of the Buddha under the Tree of Enlightenment in numbers such as these, where they turned the Wheel of Dharma in numbers such as these, where they taught and preached the Dharma in numbers such as these, where they relinquished their lives in numbers such as these, where they lay reclining on their right sides in numbers such as these, and where they entered parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without arising again in numbers such as these—all of them named Śākyamuni, their mothers named Māyā, their fathers named Śuddhodana, their lands named Kapilavastu, and their worlds named Sahā.”
Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the honored disciple Ānanda served as attendants.
As it was in the eastern direction, so it was in the nine directions; in all of them, they were Śākyamuni.

Just as it is with the number of Śākyas, so it is with those named Ti-huan-jié; so it is with those named Ti-ming-duo-luo; so it is with those named Wei-wei; so it is with those named Shi; so it is with those named Sui-ye; so it is with those named Jiu-lou-qin; so it is with those named Junahe; and so it is with those named Jiaye.
These Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, possess such gentle and subtle names as "Emitting Gentle Sounds," yet they all share the same title: Śākyamuni.
The Tathāgata perceives all this with his fully developed fleshly eye, yet even this is not worth mentioning; what he perceives is vast and exceeds these incalculable numbers.

Whether there are those who practice the Way while remaining at home or those who leave the home life to study the Way, should they cause all the bodhisattvas in a single Buddha-land to attain Buddhahood, and provide offerings to all these Buddhas for the duration of an entire kalpa—this is what is called [the merit of] "name."

Furthermore, there are those who hear this "Chapter on the Manifestation of All Buddhas" and, upon hearing it, feel joy, delight, and faith for even a brief moment; their merit surpasses that of all the people in a trichiliocosm who have attained Buddhahood and are fully provided with the requisites for making offerings.
"All Bodhisattvas who have already attained such wisdom and understanding will swiftly draw near to the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.

When this sutra was spoken, six billion two hundred million bodhisattvas attained the dharma that is difficult to fully possess; thus they attained the protection of inconceivable intent, became non-retrogressive, and were established in the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
Ten koṭis of bodhisattvas first resolved their minds upon the Great Vehicle and established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression toward unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Three billion two hundred million bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Persons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have severed all defilements, extinguished birth and death, and realized the teaching.
Countless persons shall also assemble with Maitreya.
At that time, the evil Māra, harboring a heart of malice and resentment, shed tears and addressed the Buddha:
"O World-Honored One!
It was my original vow to cause the Tathāgata to enter parinirvāṇa early, so that the people would not leave my realm.
Thus, those delivered by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, have become exceedingly numerous."
Even if his lifespan were extended to last for an eon, the number of beings he would deliver could not exceed those delivered today.
Today, the God among Gods has already vacated my realm.
Thereupon, the Buddha took a pinch of earth from the ground with two fingers and placed it upon his nail, saying to Māra:
"What do you think? Is the amount of earth on the Tathāgata’s nail more, or [the earth of the great earth]?"
"Which is more: the soil of the great earth, or [the soil on] my fingernail?
Māra addressed the Buddha, saying, "The soil on the Tathāgata’s fingernail is little, while the soil of the great earth is much, beyond measure."
The Buddha said,
"Pāpīyan! Those whom I have delivered and established in the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are as few in number as the dust upon my fingernails."
Those who follow your teaching are even more numerous than the soil of the great earth; you should therefore rejoice and be glad.
Such people as these are incalculable and cannot be exhausted.
The Buddha said to Pāpīyān:
“You wish to seek the human lineage as if seeking empty space.
Thus it is, Pāpīyān!”
"Do whatever you ought to do; at midnight tonight, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Setting aside the number of these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; setting aside all the happiness found within the lands of these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; and setting aside the flourishing of these Bodhisattvas."
He replied: "Indeed so, O God among Gods! They are all here."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If I were to spend from one eon until a hundred thousand koṭis of eons providing analogies, making comparisons, calculating, and speaking parables, lecturing on the meaning, and describing all the Buddhas, there would be no end to it; it could never be finished."

In this way, the Tathāgata perceives with his fully perfected fleshly eye all the countless Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, who currently exist; moreover, that which he sees exceeds even this, being beyond all limit.
Thereupon the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"That which the Tathāgata ought to do for all beings, he has done to deliver them all.
There is not even a thought of one who is not delivered, as small as a single hair."
"Why is this? Therefore, I tell you all.

At that time, the Buddha immediately manifested spiritual powers through a samādhi corresponding to his form, causing all the sūtras spoken by these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, to be heard by the people of this land. Those who heard this Dharma—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—established themselves in the Three Vehicles; one billion people attained the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path; ten billion people established themselves in the path of the Pratyekabuddha; and the remainder all relinquished their lives.

Chapter Seven: On the Purity of the Buddha-land. At that time, the Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics, as well as eight thousand types of excellence, ten billion voices, sixty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of languages, and infinite billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of perfected tones; possessing the marks of upholding all Buddha-dharmas, the Tathāgata’s tranquil concentration, the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses, the Tathāgata’s four bases of spiritual power, the Tathāgata’s four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas—[remained] thus.
The Tathāgata walks upon the world, causing all to behold the dharmas face-to-face;

thus, the Dharma taught by the Buddha manifests immediately, and this trichiliocosm becomes as level as the palm of a hand, free from sand, gravel, or stones, containing only mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, amber, musaragalva, gold, and silver.

Surrounding the trichiliocosm were various jeweled palaces; there were countless mansions with canopies of precious gems and *maṇi* palace-halls with canopies of jewels. Everywhere there were trees of bright moon pearls, canopies of bright moon pearls, banners and streamers of bright moon pearls, pavilions of bright moon pearls, and seats of bright moon pearls, filling the entire trichiliocosm.

Extending throughout the eight directions were eight intersecting roads, adorned with various jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, elephant-agate, amber, red *cakra* gems, auspicious merit gems, moonlight-shining gems, sun-surpassing gems, *amala* gems, *kumitra* gems, flavor gems, and emerald gems—all of which were mutually arrayed as trees, canopies, banners, and streamers.
The roots, stems, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of these trees flourished profusely, and their banners and canopies were exquisite and wondrous.
There were trees of vessels, trees of garments, and fruit-trees of necklaces, ornaments, and robes, filling the space without any gaps.
There are red sandalwood, crimson sandalwood, *jhalaka* sandalwood, and the black, wondrous-sounding *mṛgacandana*.

There were *mandārava* flowers, great *mandārava* flowers, *māndāravika* flowers, great *māndāravika* flowers, coarse flowers, great coarse flowers, soft flowers, great soft flowers, *divasaprabhāsana* flowers, great *divasaprabhāsana* flowers, *pāriyātraka* flowers, great *pāriyātraka* flowers, excellent *upapāriyātraka* flowers, moon flowers, great moon flowers, all-pervading moon flowers, *mukula* flowers, great *mukula* flowers, all-pervading *mukula* flowers, excellent *mukula* flowers, parasol flowers, great parasol flowers, all-pervading parasol flowers, fear-arising flowers, great fear-arising flowers, and all-pervading fear-arising flowers; these completely filled the trichiliocosm, leaving no empty space.
All were adorned with precious lotus flowers.
There were nine hundred and ninety billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of palatial halls, constructed of blue lapis lazuli, gold, amber, and agate.
With auspicious jewels and maṇi gems serving as wheels, and soft, exquisite garments draped over the chariot,
they pervaded the entirety of this trichiliocosm on all sides.

Within this trichiliocosm, there appeared natural lion thrones; beneath every tree there was a natural lion throne, furnished with exquisite cushions of fine silk, brocade, and the most sublime garments.
There were variegated net-curtains, their patterns interlaced like sash-ornaments, some adorned with golden-flame mani-jewels.
Upon all the lion-thrones sat bodhisattvas, their bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

This trichiliocosm was completely covered on all sides with red pearls, blue pearls, and white pearls; there were red sandalwood petals, *madhugandha* incense, and exquisite black incense, scattered over with fine gold dust.
Thereupon, throughout the void of space above the trichiliocosm, there were canopies of mani-jewel nets everywhere, from which issued the sounds of celestial music.
Jewels were suspended upon these canopies, including exquisite *sūtra-maṇi* jewels, *sūtra-śikhara-maṇi* jewels, *siṃha-lalita-maṇi* jewels, and *cakra-lakṣma-maṇi* jewels.
It was bound with cords of interwoven golden threads; it was adorned with various gold ornaments as jeweled canopies and curtains, and the canopies and curtains were made of pure gold.

This [structure] surrounded the entire trichiliocosm, extending from the surface of the earth below up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three above, and was further adorned all around with *maṇi* jewels and purple-burnished gold.
From the golden pavilion issued forth countless billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of exquisite sounds: the sound of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the sound of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; the sound of tranquility, morality, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
the sound of self-discipline, humility, patience, and shame; and the sound of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

The sound of practicing with composure; the sound of giving and the sound of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*); the sound of ethical discipline and the sound of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*);
the sound of patience and the sound of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*); the sound of diligence and the sound of the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*);
the sound of single-mindedness and the sound of the perfection of single-mindedness (*dhyānapāramitā*); the sound of wisdom... [the sound of] wisdom.
The sound of the perfection of wisdom; the sound of supernormal powers and the sound of the perfection of supernormal powers; the sound of the bodhisattva practices;
the sound of bringing bodhisattvas to the stage of non-retrogression; the sound of bodhisattvas attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas;
and the sound of all the Buddhas' teachings.
It is like the radiance of Amitābha Buddha in the land of Sumati; it is like that of the World-Honored One Akṣobhya, and as supreme and exquisite as all that exists in the land of Gandhavatī.

As with the Jewel-Fragrance God among gods, as with the World-Hero of the Buddha-realm of Dharma-Flame-Light, as with the World-Honored One Maṇi-Rāja, as with Sūrya-Ratnagarbha and likewise Sūrya-Ratnagarbha, as with Ghoṣarāja Buddha, as with Sugata Buddha, and as the flourishing and peaceful prosperity of the Buddha-realm of Sumerukalpa, so too is the flourishing and joyful prosperity of the land of the Lion of the Śākyas.
Out of compassion for all beings, he manifests parinirvāṇa so that people may know this without doubt.
Because the Buddha-fields of the World-Honored One are impoverished, out of compassion for such as these, he manifests lands of bliss.
Just as all Buddhas, the Honored Ones, perform the deeds of the Buddha-way, so it is in the realm of Śākyasiṃha; there is not even a hair’s breadth of difference, neither more nor less.
Furthermore, just as all Buddha-lands possess joy, adornment, purity, and excellence, so it is in the realm of Śākyasiṃha; there is not even a hair’s breadth of disparity.
Chapter Eight: The Deva-Bodhisattva Chapter At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha wept with deep sorrow and spoke these verses:

“Like the full moon dwelling in the void, Or like the sun’s gentle thousand rays of light, Or like fire and mani-jewels illuminating all— The World-Honored One shall no longer enter into instruction.”
Who will henceforth protect the worlds, as countless beings wander through birth and death?
All the worlds have become blind and dark, because the World-Honored One has entered the space between the trees.
All classes of sentient beings throughout the triple world, whatever peace and happiness they may obtain,
all receive it through the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Honored Sangha, who bear their sorrows and provide them with nurture.
The Lion of the Śākyas, the skillful King of Physicians, who heals the suffering of grief and carries beings to the further shore—
having exhorted all to cross over their manifold hardships, the Dharma King has entered between the twin trees.
The entire world shall fall into madness, for they do not see the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas;
having removed immeasurable lust, anger, and delusion, the people will stare in daze and suddenly collapse to the ground.
The God among Gods extinguishes birth and death; The golden-winged dragon-birds all take refuge in him.
The ghosts, asuras, and mahoragas— After the World-Honored One has departed, they all fall into darkness.
Free from lust and having left behind the dust of pride, his radiance illuminating the four quarters has now ceased;
all the world shall fall into great darkness—what can be done when the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa?

After Anuruddha had spoken this verse, at that very moment various devas arrived, some riding in chariots, some traveling alone, some riding elephants, some riding horse-drawn carriages, some in open-latticed chariots, some on seats, some in palaces, some at windows, some in curtained pavilions, some above doors, some on crescent-shaped balconies, and some on stairways; each descended from their respective vehicle or from where they were stationed.
Having descended, he wept and wailed with lamentation, went to the birthplace of the Mallas, and upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Some devas scattered blue, red, yellow, and white *utpala* lotuses; others scattered various types of sandalwood.
There were some devas who took their own jeweled crowns, jeweled pendants, the jewels upon their hands, and celestial robes, scattering them over the Buddha as an offering to him.
Then, the Venerable Rāhula, weeping with deep sorrow, spoke these verses:
"With virtues most extraordinary and immeasurable wisdom, You are honored by the multitude and dispel all delusion."
Having eliminated all evil, toil, and sorrow, he has entered the birthplace of the Malla heroes.
The Buddha is a field of merit for all to revere; the Honored One is a King of Physicians who extinguishes all ailments.
The Honored One’s marks and features are as beautiful as a lotus flower; the Honored One now lies reclining amidst the trees.
The Buddha surpasses the sun and moon throughout all worlds; his immeasurable radiance eclipses the light of the heavens.
As the Lord of Dharma, he exceeds Mount Sumeru, delivering hundreds of millions of people from their diligent toil and suffering.
The Buddha has entered the dharma of emptiness, tranquil and non-existent;
having reached the further shore of supreme non-conception, the Honored One has cast aside all worldly aspirations, and the Dharma King has now entered among the trees.
The World-Honored One’s eye extinguishes the darkness of the world;
with the threefold knowledge unimpeded regarding past, future, and present, the Buddha acts as a guide to deliver beings from birth and death; out of compassion, the Buddha rests beneath the tree.
The Honored One utters a sublime sound with a lion’s roar; the Buddha’s speech is as bright as the moon’s illumination.
The Buddha’s gentle resonance brings joy to all; out of compassion, the Buddha rests beneath the trees.
The wise Rāhula, extolling the One of Ten Powers, suddenly became dazed and fell prostrate upon the ground;
rolling about on the earth, he beat his breast and cried out: "O King of Dharma, have compassion! Do not enter parinirvāṇa!"

After the Venerable Rāhula had spoken this verse, at that very moment, in the eastern direction, there were inconceivable, innumerable, ineffable, and boundless worlds where the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, [resided].

Countless, incalculable, inconceivable, and limitless bodhisattvas from various lands have taken their leave of their respective Buddhas and arrived at this realm, desiring to see the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa and the great assembly of bodhisattvas; they wish to behold the Tathāgata, prostrate themselves, kneel, pay homage, and serve him with offerings.

As the bodhisattvas passed through the worlds they traversed, which were countless and immeasurable, all the celestial palaces resounded with divine music that played spontaneously without being struck, and rains of celestial incense and celestial flowers fell.

In those various worlds, there were sons of gods of great virtue who had studied the Mahāyāna, as well as kings of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, all of whom followed the bodhisattvas as attendants to come and make offerings.

Bodhisattvas came adorned with various jewels; some came wearing the robes of devaputras, some in the attire of devaputras of the sixth heaven, some in the attire of Brahmā-devas, some in the attire of Vaśavartin devaputras, some in the attire of Sunirmita devaputras, some in the attire of Tuṣita devaputras, some in the attire of Śakra-devendra, some in the attire of Sūryadevaputra, and some in the attire of Candrarāja. Some Bodhisattvas came entering into mani-jewel palaces and sitting cross-legged; some came entering into mani-jewel mansions and sitting there; and some came entering into mani-jewel latticed canopies and sitting there.

Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas who came entering through fragrant halls, fragrant palaces, and fragrant canopies of interlaced jewels, where they sat cross-legged; some came entering through halls of purple-polished gold, some entering through palaces of every kind of jewel, and some entering through canopies of every kind of jewel interlaced with jewels, where they sat cross-legged.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas who came having entered chambers of red sandalwood or various sandalwood palaces, sitting cross-legged within them.

There were also bodhisattvas who came having entered palaces of seven-jeweled flowers, or palaces of *maṇi* jewels whose moonlight was more radiant than the sun and moon, or palaces of wish-fulfilling jewels, or wish-fulfilling jewel mansions, or canopies of interlaced *maṇi* wish-fulfilling jewels, where they sat cross-legged.
All these bodhisattvas adorn their bodies with the thirty-two marks; they possess countless radiances and inconceivable splendors, as well as countless vast luminosities.
That radiance removes the diligent suffering of all people and causes them all to obtain the radiance of wholesome thoughts.

It is the radiance that removes [the realms of] all hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; it is the radiance that leads all beings to the good paths. It causes the body to possess merit and the marks of excellence, making it upright and beautiful; those who see it rejoice and love its color, such that none can equal it, and its form is beheld by all.

There is the Brahma-voice with its gentle resonance, the sound that causes all beings on the various paths to rejoice, the sound that terrifies all Māras, the sound that benefits all people, the sound that brings forth all dharmas and all merits, and the sound that extinguishes all evils and emits the immeasurable light of the Dharma.
There were bodhisattva mahāsattvas there who rained down various celestial flowers of precious jewels, covering the entire trichiliocosm as they approached the Tathāgata.

Some rained down garments; some rained down necklaces and ornaments; some rained down parasols; some rained down banners and streamers; some rained down various types of sandalwood; some rained down purple-gold; some rained down lotus flowers; some rained down wish-fulfilling jewels; and some rained down all manner of treasures surpassing those of the heavens, descending throughout the trichiliocosm to reach the Tathāgata.
There may be bodhisattvas who manifest various precious ornamental canopies as vast as a trichiliocosm, surpassing all celestial jewels, to offer them to the Tathāgata.

There are some bodhisattvas who, adorned with various necklaces and ornaments, manifest lotus flowers as vast as a trichiliocosm; they have wheels made of fine roots of blue lapis lazuli, musaragalva, amber, and *śrīgarbha* jewels, with wish-fulfilling jewel chariots pervading everywhere, all exquisitely decorated with flaming-light *maṇi* gems and gold.

Some manifested a palace as vast as a trichiliocosm; others manifested jeweled canopies surpassing those of the heavens, as vast as a trichiliocosm, adorned entirely with flaming-light pearls and gold.
Or there may be those who manifest pure realms as vast as a trichiliocosm—immensely great, incalculable, infinite, inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless.

The beings to be converted were thus: they came from the eight directions, above and below, in such numbers that they were incalculable, innumerable, inconceivable, and immeasurable—all these bodhisattvas came to make offerings to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

All these bodhisattvas simultaneously came forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated the World-Honored One three times. Each, from their respective direction, manifested a great lotus lion throne adorned with various jewel-flame light pearls and gold.

Each and every bodhisattva, for the sake of the Buddha, manifested a lion throne between the twin trees. Upon it, they spread immeasurable, pure celestial *kāṣāya* robes. They adorned them with countless varieties of colors—immeasurable colors, incalculable colors, and hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* incalculable colors—surpassing all that exists in the heavens. Canopies were fashioned from flaming-light pearls, yellow gold, and various jewels such as purple-gold, serving as magnificent ornaments. They were perfumed with fragrances surpassing those of the heavens, causing the various evil realms to conceive the original thought of goodness and making all beings joyful and delighted.
Just as the adornments manifested by one bodhisattva are so, so too are those of all bodhisattvas;
yet the respective transformations of each individual bodhisattva do not intermingle or overlap.
Why is this? Because they are tranquil and free from flattery and deceit, and have no attachment to any phenomena.
They are like a wish-fulfilling jewel, which cannot be defiled by any dust or impurities.

They train in skillful means and expedients; their mindfulness regarding all phenomena is pure; they attain the dharmas of the noble ones' wisdom. As it is with their bodily conduct, so it is with their speech. They act as great masters of giving, abiding in the Dharma without attachment.
All these bodhisattvas praised the Tathāgata’s original quest for the Way—his incalculable, boundless, immeasurable, and ineffable ascetic practices—and manifested them through their true meaning.
Chapter Nine: The Tathāgata’s Transformation and Preaching of the Dharma At that time, the Venerable Ānanda praised the Buddha in verse, saying:
“Your eyes are clear and pure like the full moon; With the ten powers, spiritual feet, and wisdom free from dust, You are served by devas and nāga kings;
Today, the World-Honored One has entered among the trees.”
When the Buddha and his assembly enter the great city together, as the Hero of the World steps upon the threshold of the gate,
heaven and earth tremble in six ways, and he radiates light that pervades the Buddha-lands.
Lutes, harps, flutes, drums, and all manner of musical instruments, though unplayed,
spontaneously produce soft and gentle sounds; lions, tigers, deer, and wild oxen, as well as various dragons and great elephants dwelling on the Snowy Mountains,
roar and bellow upon the land with hearts full of joy, all directing thoughts of loving-kindness toward the Tathāgata.

Their voices were delightful and surpassed all precious jewels; hundreds of thousands of nayutas of oxen, seeing the Buddha’s radiance, all leaped for joy, attaining immeasurable peace and countless bliss.
Cranes, ducks, cormorants, geese, and *kroñca* birds, as well as *ara*, *cañcu*, and countless other multitudes,
including parrots from the Iron Ring Mountains, came to the Buddha’s dwelling, chirping with joyful exultation.
The various treasuries of jewels that people had originally lost were all recovered upon reaching the World-Honored One;
those who harbored anger all came to possess a heart of loving-kindness, and with pure minds, they served the Buddha.
The devas dwelling in the void rained down celestial flowers;
furthermore, lotuses with a thousand petals appeared, as the palace ladies and the sons of gods each made offerings to the World-Honored One.
When the purity of form thus ceases to appear, and the Buddha is now about to enter *nirvāṇa*, what shall we do?
It is like a calf being cut off from its mother’s milk; the severance of this protection is most grievous.
Throughout the ten directions, they have been free from defilement from the beginning; having already transcended birth and death, they are the protectors of all beings.
As the heroes of the world, they exercise sovereignty over the realms, and their attainment remains steadfast for incalculable eons.
Who is the Radiant King who surpasses the sun and moon?
Who possesses strength that exceeds the Iron Mountains?
Who possesses patience equal to the earth?
The World-Honored One guides people to leave behind the dust of the world; through diligence and single-mindedness, he manifests wisdom to deliver all.

If a son were separated from his mother for a hundred million lifetimes, meeting her but once before parting again, the son would grieve and search for his kin in the four directions—so it is with me regarding the World-Honored One’s nirvana.
Filled with sorrow and diligent toil, there is no longer any joy;
seeing the places where the Buddha walked and sat, as well as the lecture halls and monasteries—alas, how can this state of misfortune ever come to an end?

Praising the one who bestows the gift of Dharma throughout the ten directions, the virtuous Śākyaputra of immeasurable diligence and toil, he then fell prostrate upon the ground, rolling to and fro; "I am the foremost among those who perceive the Moon, the Virtuous Moon."
At that time, the World-Honored One, through the Samādhi of Holding All Phrases, the Samādhi of Manifesting Peaceful Conduct through Right Concentration,
the Samādhi of Skillful Exposition, the Samādhi of Thunder and Rain, the Samādhi of the Lion’s Roar,
the Samādhi of Radiant Resonance, the Samādhi of Majestic Splendor and Light, the Samādhi of Emitting Light, and the Subtle and Wondrous [Samādhi]...
The Samādhi of Phrases, the Samādhi of Powers, the Samādhi of the Phrase of Powers, the Samādhi of Infinite Power,
the Samādhi of the Radiant Illumination of the Mind-Holding, the Samādhi of Arising in the World, the Samādhi of Drum-Sound, the Samādhi of the Moon,
the Samādhi of the Great Moon, the Samādhi of the Circumambient Moon, the Samādhi of the Moon’s Resonance, and the Samādhi of the Upper Moon.
The Samādhi of Obscurity, the Samādhi of the Treasury, the Samādhi of the Treasury of Truths, the Samādhi of Lapis Lazuli Treasury, the Samādhi of Contemplation,
the Samādhi of Immeasurable Contemplation, the Samādhi of Universally Illuminating All Ten Directions,
the Samādhi of the Light that Removes All Doubts, the Samādhi of Sincerity, the Samādhi of Truthful Sincerity, and the Samādhi of Ultimate Speech.
The Samādhi, the Samādhi of Explaining All Phenomena, the Samādhi of Truthful Sincerity as Spoken,
the Immeasurable Samādhi, the Tranquil Samādhi, the Samādhi of the Phrase of Tranquility, the Samādhi of Truthful and Tranquil Speech,
the Samādhi of Giving, the Samādhi of Truthful Giving, the Samādhi of the Great Giver, and the Radiance.
The Samādhi of Illumination, the Samādhi of Excellent Radiance, the Samādhi of Great Radiance, the Samādhi of Immeasurable Radiance,
the Samādhi of the Illuminating Phrase, the Samādhi of the Radiance that Severs All Doubt, the Samādhi of Expounding the Roots of All Goodness,
the Samādhi of Eliminating and Expounding the Bonds of Doubt, the Samādhi of Truthfully Expounding Vision, and—

These are the samādhi of severing doubt, the samādhi of skillfully bestowing cessation and understanding, the samādhi of manifesting all Buddhas, the samādhi of manifesting the teaching of all practices,
the samādhi of skillfully teaching all practices, the samādhi of skillfully teaching the turning of the wheel of Dharma,
and the samādhi of skillfully opening and delivering beings in their respective places; by means of these, one skillfully teaches the wisdom of the present Buddhas.

In the state of dwelling within the samādhi of right reception, from each and every pore there emerge hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lights—incalculable, inconceivable, ineffable, immeasurable, and boundless.
At the tip of each light, there are manifested countless, inconceivable, and immeasurable bathing pools; from each bathing pool, there are further manifested [lotuses].
He manifested countless, infinite billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of lotuses; upon each and every lotus,
he conjured countless, infinite billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of seats,
and upon all these seats sat Tathāgatas preaching the Dharma.

Each of these manifested Tathāgatas guides those people, causing them to establish themselves on the stage of non-retrogression and abide in the Buddha-dharma; their number is equal to that of the manifested Buddhas seated upon the lotuses, who have attained the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat.

Each of these groups is equal in number to that of the pratyekabuddhas; likewise, those who have attained non-retrogression and established the roots of goodness are equal in number, as are those born in the heavens who no longer undergo suffering.

At the edge of each bathing pool there were four jeweled trees, with countless trunks, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits. Upon every single trunk, node, branch, leaf, flower, and fruit, there were manifested countless, inconceivable, and immeasurable Tathāgatas; these emanations sat upon lion thrones, preaching the Dharma to deliver all beings.
Their number was equal to the number of Tathāgatas upon the manifested trees.
Having brought all beings to liberation, they then spoke this verse:
"The World-Honored One, the Most Honored among Men, Has attained perfect awakening to all things."
Those who see him with joy all abandon the evil realms.
Having long possessed supernormal powers, this Hero of the World is difficult to encounter;
he is like the udumbara flower, his appearance pleasing and beautiful.
Those who wish to make offerings to the Buddha, and those who wish to serve my own person—
upon hearing this Dharma of the sutra, their hearts shall be filled with joy.
Those who wish to see the World-Honored One, the supreme among men, in the present—
The World’s Radiance and Majestic Power— one should have faith in and delight in this auspiciousness.
As for all the Buddhas yet to come, who shall guide and lead people with their light;
if you wish to see these World-Honored Ones, you should have faith in this auspiciousness.
Those who seek the Great Vehicle shall attain great benefit;
having heard this Dharma of the sutra, they shall serve the Buddha.
Their eyes will attain purity, as will their faculties of ear and nose.
The faculties of body, speech, and mind are severed and free from grasping;
Samādhi and precepts are pure, and wisdom and liberation are pure.
The knowledge that manifests liberation is the realization of truth.
"Having understood all phenomena, No self-conception arises within me;
What is known is neither extinguished nor increased, And thus I do not grieve over echoes.

After these verses of the Tathāgata of Emanations were spoken, immeasurable people at that moment established themselves in the Three Vehicles. The inhabitants of countless worlds all attained single-mindedness. All hells in countless Buddha-lands were completely extinguished; all animals were liberated from their toil and suffering; and all hungry ghosts attained peace and security.
At that time, the Buddha entered the meditative absorption of the "Jewels of Measure" (*pramāṇa-ratna-samādhi-samāpatti*).

When the Tathāgata dwells in this samādhi, according to whatever jewels each person desires to obtain, they are granted exactly as they wish; they see the treasures of the Buddha-land all appearing before them, and they see the various Buddha-trees adorned with jewels. According to their inclinations and the colors they wish to see, they see the various provinces, kingdoms, districts, towns, and the people of those lands, such that the entire Buddha-land appears filled with these things, just as they desire.

For as long as life lasts, whenever they wish to see various adornments, they will see at will men, women, boys, and girls adorned with necklaces and ornaments; they will likewise see devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
Whatever clothing they desire, whatever food and drink they desire, and whatever dwellings they desire—all that which accords with their inclinations is seen and obtained.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"There is a samādhi called 'Wisdom-Practice' (Prajñācaryā). When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, abide in this samādhi, they obtain a samādhi according to the desires of beings; thus, as they wish, they immediately see all the aspirations of people."

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called the Samādhi of Immeasurable Transcendence. It is auspicious and majestic; according to whatever one desires, one obtains all things, which immediately appear before one as wished for. Having obtained these things, one makes offerings to the Tathāgata.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "the Eye. When they abide in this samādhi, they cause all people to no longer practice desire, but instead to delight in the desire for the Way and virtue; they no longer practice impure thoughts regarding sexual desire, nor do they take pleasure in it even in their dreams.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Mental Shame and Remorse. When they abide in this samādhi, they cause all the people within their Buddha-fields to possess a sense of shame and remorse, and to be free from anger and distracted thoughts.
Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi named *Cakṣur-mukha*; by abiding in this samādhi, the blind obtain their eyes. Ānanda!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Lord of Sorrowlessness. When they abide in this samādhi, if they enter a city, they cause all people there to be free from further sorrow and affliction.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Lord of Supernatural Powers. Abiding in this samādhi, they cause those who lack supernatural powers to fly through the air, with their spiritual feet able to rise as high as seven trees.
Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "World-Illumination. When they abide in this samādhi, those who are blind are able to see the World-Honored One. Ānanda!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Receiving Purity. When they abide in this samādhi and step upon the threshold of the gate, they cause all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharva kings, asura kings, garuḍa kings, kiṃnara kings, mahoraga kings, Śakra, and Brahmā to prostrate themselves there in worship of the Buddha.

Ānanda, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Surpassing the Lion’s Brilliance. When they abide in this samādhi, all those of other heterodox paths who behold the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power are subdued and take refuge in him.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called Vajra-Light. When they abide in this samādhi and step upon the earth, the three thousand great thousandfold world-systems—including the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains, Sumeru the king of mountains, and the Black Mountains; all the ravines, pits, valleys, mountain forests, and the ground itself—all become level. That which was high becomes low, and the mounds and ruins become flat; the ground becomes as soft as fine cloth.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Subduing the Powers of Māra. When they abide in this samādhi, they cause all Māras to be terrified, alarmed, and restless; each of them finds no joy in their own palaces, and their fear does not cease until they see the Buddha, take refuge in him, and thus prostrate themselves at his feet.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Fearlessness. When they abide in this samādhi, they cause all people to have no intent to harm one another; they are free from all fears and devoid of arrogance.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Exquisite Phrases. When they abide in this samādhi, they cause all people in the various worlds who have no food to obtain countless varieties of flavors.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Color. When they abide in this samādhi, they cause all people to obtain excellent and wondrous physical forms and no longer suffer from many illnesses.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Causing Those Without Clothes to Obtain Natural Garments Spontaneously. When dwelling in this samādhi, those imprisoned in hell all attain liberation; those in distress and calamity are freed from their suffering and obtain peace and happiness; the stingy and greedy take delight in giving; those with corrupt precepts abide in pure morality; the wrathful establish themselves in patience; the indolent are made diligent; they sever all unwholesome dharmas and cultivate the increase of wholesome dharmas; those with distracted minds attain one-pointed concentration; and those with inferior wisdom attain pure wisdom.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Expounding the Words of Skillful Speech on the Absence of Volitional Activity. When they abide in this samādhi, all who are sorrowful are made to leap with joy.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi named "Twofold Light. When abiding in this samādhi, they encounter no obstruction regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present, and there is no wisdom that they do not manifest with equal clarity.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a samādhi called "Free from Deceit Regarding All Dharmas. When they abide in this samādhi, they cause the bodhisattva mahāsattvas to attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda, the noble disciples, the bodhisattvas assembled from the ten directions, the devas, nāgas, and spirits, and the people of the world paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
